Reverse-shell egress from netcat/shell child of Flowise (CVE-2026-69256 C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the outbound callback of the CVE-2026-69256 reverse shell: after os.system launches nc/sh, that child makes an outbound connection to the attacker's listener (PoC uses port 13337). Flags nc/ncat/netcat or an interactive shell binary initiating a connection to a public IP on a Flowise server, which should never happen. Rationale: Targets the article's reverse-shell callback — nc ... -e /bin/sh reaching a public listener — using the child process (nc/shell) initiating outbound to a non-RFC1918 address as the pivot, a distinct network-telemetry angle from the process-spawn detection (UC2). Interactive shells/netcat egressing from a headless AI-agent server is inherently high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3hjv-c53m-58jj
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit ops use of nc for outbound port testing to an internet host (filter -z/-w probes at process layer)
  • SSH-tunnel or backup scripts using bash with /dev/tcp to an external endpoint
  • Monitoring agents wrapping curl/nc to reach a public status endpoint
  • Container debugging where an operator manually runs nc from a shell
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the remote IP:port and whois/geo it; confirm the initiating binary is nc/shell and trace its parent to the Flowise node PID. 2) Contain: block the destination IP:port egress, isolate the host, and terminate the reverse-shell session. 3) Hunt: check the destination IP across all hosts for other beacons, pull the matching inbound /api/v1/prediction request (UC1), and confirm patch level of flowise/flowise-components (>3.1.2).

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","nc.traditional","sh","bash","dash","zsh")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc

Flowise node process spawning shell/recon commands (CVE-2026-69255 Pyodide RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-69255 CSV Agent Pyodide injection where the Flowise Node.js server reaches child_process via `process.mainModule.constructor._load('child_process').execSync(...)` and spawns an OS shell. The proof-of-concept executes `id`/`uname -a` as root (PID 1) in the container, so this surfaces the Flowise `node` parent spawning a shell or recon binary it should never launch. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact exploit primitive — the Flowise `node` server reaching child_process.execSync and spawning `id`/`uname -a` (the PoC recon commands, which contain no commas per the `csvFile.split(',')` constraint). Parent=node + shell/recon child is the observable that the in-memory Pyodide injection produces on the host. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmv7-4m6c-3cg5 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-69255
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise container entrypoint (docker-entrypoint.sh) legitimately launching node then a shell during startup
  • npm/yarn lifecycle scripts under node_modules spawning sh -c for install hooks
  • Health-check probes that shell out via node for readiness checks
  • Admins running `docker exec` recon inside the Flowise container
  • Custom Flowise tool/agent nodes that legitimately shell out
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "node_modules" and ProcessCommandLine !has "docker-entrypoint" and ProcessCommandLine !has "npm"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine — a bare `id`, `uname -a`, `whoami`, or `cat /proc/1/environ` under a `node` parent whose cmdline references flowise is high-fidelity RCE. Confirm the container/host runs Flowise <= 3.1.2. 2) Contain: isolate the Flowise container/host, rotate FLOWISE_PASSWORD and any API keys under /root/.flowise, and block egress. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same aid/DeviceName for outbound port-4444 connections (UC2) and reads of /root/.flowise (UC3); review Flowise chatflow-creation logs for the attacker's CSV Agent flow ID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","uname","whoami","cat")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("flowise","Flowise","flowise-components")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "/node" or ParentProcessName =~ "node"
| where ActingProcessName endswith "/sh" or ActingProcessName endswith "/bash" or ActingProcessName endswith "/dash" or ActingProcessName endswith "/id" or ActingProcessName endswith "/uname" or ActingProcessName endswith "/whoami" or ActingProcessName endswith "/cat"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("flowise","Flowise","flowise-components")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise node process reverse shell / C2 egress (Meterpreter post-exploit) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the C2 stage of CVE-2026-69255 where the exploited Flowise container establishes a Meterpreter reverse_tcp session. The verified PoC calls back to the Metasploit default port 4444; this surfaces outbound connections to 4444 (or the docker-bridge callback) initiated by the Flowise node process or a shell child it spawned. Rationale: The article's Metasploit proof shows a Meterpreter reverse_tcp session on the default 4444 listener initiated from the exploited container; port 4444 sourced from `node` or a shell child is a low-FP C2 signal. Sentinel path uses ImNetworkSession's DstPortNumber (ImNetworkSession has no process column, so process scoping is dropped there and pushed onto EDR sources). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmv7-4m6c-3cg5 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-69255
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1059.004 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned red-team / pentest Metasploit listeners on 4444
  • Developers running local Metasploit or CTF labs on the same subnet
  • Legitimate app coincidentally bound to 4444 (rare)
  • Vulnerability scanners emulating reverse-shell callbacks
  • QA reproducing the Flowise CVE in a test environment
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIPType == "Private" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("msfconsole","metasploit","pentest"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process (node or shell child of node/flowise) and the remote IP — an internal docker-bridge gateway (e.g. 172.17.0.1) or external host on 4444 with a preceding UC1 hit is a confirmed session. 2) Contain: kill the process, isolate the container/host, and drop the 4444 egress at the firewall. 3) Hunt: search all Flowise hosts for the same remote IP on any port, review reads of /root/.flowise (UC3), and audit chatflow creation for the attacker-created CSV Agent flow.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","sh","bash","dash")
| where RemotePort == 4444
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 4444
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcPortNumber, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flowise credential/DB access under /root/.flowise by shell child (CVE-2026-69255 post-exploit) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts post-exploitation credential theft in CVE-2026-69255, where the root shell reads FLOWISE_PASSWORD and the SQLite database at DATABASE_PATH=/root/.flowise. Legit access to that path comes from the `node` server itself, so this flags a shell/recon binary (sh, cat, env) touching the Flowise secrets directory. Rationale: Uses the article's disclosed secrets location — DATABASE_PATH=/root/.flowise and FLOWISE_PASSWORD — as the crown-jewel path. Scoping the initiating process to shell/recon binaries (not `node`, which legitimately owns that DB) isolates hands-on-keyboard credential theft from normal Flowise operation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmv7-4m6c-3cg5 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-69255
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/cron jobs (tar, rsync via sh) archiving the /root/.flowise data directory
  • Admin troubleshooting the Flowise SQLite DB with cat/sqlite3
  • Container image-build steps copying config
  • Log-rotation scripts touching the directory
  • Monitoring agents reading DB size
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "rsync" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "tar" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "backup"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the shell child and its cmdline — `cat /root/.flowise/*.sqlite`, `env | grep FLOWISE`, or `cat /proc/1/environ` under a shell parented by node/flowise is confirmed credential theft. Correlate with a UC1 process-spawn hit on the same host. 2) Contain: rotate FLOWISE_PASSWORD, all stored chatflow API keys, and the DB encryption secret; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 for 4444 egress and check whether the stolen DB/API keys were used against downstream LLM providers or integrations referenced in the chatflows.

Flowise/node process spawning Unix shell or netcat reverse shell (CVE-2026-69254 vm2 escape) AIInstallation High
Hunts the on-host manifestation of the CVE-2026-69254 vm2 sandbox escape: the Flowise 'node' process spawning /bin/sh, bash, nc, ncat or socat with reverse-shell markers. A node-parent-to-shell edge carrying /dev/tcp or nc -e is the highest-fidelity signal of the escape reaching child_process. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact escape endpoint (node child_process launching a reverse shell) and the PoC's nc pattern to 172.17.0.1:1337; node-parent-to-shell with /dev/tcp or nc -e is a rare, high-fidelity edge. Cross-checked vm2-escape-to-child_process behaviour against the vm2 advisory wave and Flowise active-exploitation reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3769-jgqc-cxm7 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/vm2-nodejs-library-vulnerabilities.html • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/http/flowise_js_rce/
ATT&CKT1211 T1059.004 T1059.007 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based build tooling (node-gyp, prebuild, npm/yarn lifecycle scripts) forking sh -c during image builds
  • Flowise/node worker legitimately shelling out to ffmpeg/imagemagick/git via child_process for document processing
  • Container healthcheck scripts using nc to test port reachability of a downstream service
  • Developer or CI running a node app interactively that spawns bash for a subprocess helper
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","npm ","yarn ","node_modules/.bin","/usr/bin/ffmpeg","convert ","git ")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and the node parent's InitiatingProcessCommandLine; confirm the shell/nc invocation carries a reverse-shell shape (/dev/tcp, -e /bin/sh, mkfifo) and identify the remote endpoint. Check whether the host runs Flowise and is internet-reachable. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/container, kill the node and child shell PIDs, and block the observed remote IP:port at the egress firewall. Rotate any secrets (E2B/API keys, DB creds) reachable from the Flowise process. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the node PID for outbound connections (UC2), review Flowise API/auth logs for the preceding AgentAsTool/baseURL config change, and search other Flowise hosts for the same parent-child edge.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","netcat","nc.traditional","socat")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("child_process","/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo")
| where FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","nc.traditional","socat")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","npm ","yarn ","node_modules/.bin"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","child_process")
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","node_modules/.bin"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Reverse-shell egress from Flowise node process tree (nc/shell child dialing out) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the C2 leg of CVE-2026-69254: an outbound TCP connection initiated by a shell, netcat, socat, python or perl process whose PARENT is node/Flowise. Interactive shells and netcat under a node service should not originate network connections, so this parent-scoped egress is a strong reverse-shell indicator regardless of the specific attacker IP. Rationale: Uses the article's reverse-shell C2 leg (nc/shell child of node connecting outbound, PoC to 172.17.0.1:1337); scoping the connecting process by node parentage keeps it Flowise-specific and durable to IP/port rotation. Sentinel left empty because its ASIM ImNetworkSession has no reliable acting-process attribution for Linux egress in this tenant, so the node-parent scoping cannot be expressed there. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3769-jgqc-cxm7 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html
ATT&CKT1571 T1059.004 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node app whose child python/perl helper legitimately fetches from an internal HTTP API on a non-standard port
  • Container init/entrypoint shell running curl-like health probes via nc to a service mesh sidecar
  • Monitoring/APM agent spawned under node that beacons to a collector on a custom port
  • Developer debugging a node service that manually launches python for an outbound test
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","perl") and RemoteIPType == "Private" and RemotePort in (8080, 8000, 9090))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the connecting process is a shell/nc/socat whose parent is node and capture the remote IP:port; enrich the destination against threat intel and check if it is internal vs external. Correlate to a matching UC1 process-spawn hit on the same host/PID. 2) CONTAIN: Block the destination at egress, isolate the container/host, and terminate the node parent plus the connecting child. 3) HUNT: Sweep all Flowise hosts for the same shell-under-node egress shape, review Flowise auth and node-config API logs for the AgentAsTool baseURL injection that preceded it, and check for secondary tooling downloads over the channel.

Flowise API exploitation: path-traversal / JS-injection payloads to /api/v1 endpoints (CVE-2026-69254) AIDelivery Low
Hunts inbound exploitation of CVE-2026-69254 at the web tier: requests to a Flowise instance's /api/v1 (auth, tool-config, prediction) endpoints carrying the moment CVE-2022-24785 traversal string (../../../etc/passwd) or vm2/baseURL injection markers (nodeVMOptions, useSandbox, child_process). Requires a WAF/reverse proxy that inspects and logs request bodies, since the injection lands in the AgentAsTool baseURL JSON config. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete exploit primitives — the moment path-traversal string (../../../etc/passwd from CVE-2022-24785) and the AgentAsTool baseURL/nodeVMOptions injection surface — scoped to Flowise /api/v1 endpoints. Marked Low/hunting because the payload rides in the POST body, so it only surfaces where a WAF logs bodies (Message field); Defender/Datadog/Falcon left empty as none ship web-proxy body telemetry here. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3769-jgqc-cxm7 • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/http/flowise_js_rce/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/flowise-ai-agent-builder-under-active.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Burp) probing the Flowise host with traversal and injection test strings
  • Internal red-team / pentest validation of CVE-2026-69254 against a staging Flowise instance
  • Legitimate AgentAsTool configs whose baseURL happens to contain encoded path segments
  • WAF replaying or logging blocked-request signatures that contain the traversal token from its own ruleset
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0") and RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","Burp","zgrab")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the request targeted a real Flowise instance and whether it was allowed or blocked by the WAF; extract SourceIP, the endpoint, and the payload, and check whether the source is a sanctioned scanner. 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned and allowed, block the source IP at the WAF, and on the Flowise host check for the UC1/UC2 process-spawn and egress hits that would confirm the escape succeeded; isolate the host if so. 3) HUNT: Review Flowise auth logs for the POST /api/v1/auth/login that preceded the config change, enumerate AgentAsTool/ChatflowTool/ExecuteFlow nodes for injected baseURL values, and confirm the instance is patched past Flowise 3.1.1 / not running vm2 with useSandbox:false.

Flowise node process spawning shell/netcat (TypeORM DataSource RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Flowise server process (node) spawning a Unix shell or netcat/socat, which is the execution primitive of the CVE-2026-69251 TypeORM DataSource entity-load RCE. The uploaded JS entity runs `process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('/usr/bin/nc ... -e /bin/sh')`, so the running node service becomes the parent of nc/sh. Rationale: Uses the article's exact execution chain — node (Flowise server) invoking child_process to run '/usr/bin/nc 172.17.0.1 1337 -e /bin/sh'. Parent=node + child nc/socat (or shell with -e/dev-tcp reverse-shell markers) is near-zero in normal Flowise operation. Cross-checked against elttam's multi-flaw Flowise disclosure covering TypeORM DataSource entity loading. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g32j-mmxr-gfq5 • https://www.cryptika.com/six-flowise-rce-flaws-let-attackers-execute-code-on-ai-workflow-servers/ • https://typeorm.io/docs/data-source/data-source/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • npm/yarn postinstall lifecycle scripts where node spawns sh -c to run a build step
  • A container entrypoint wrapper that has node exec a shell for health checks
  • Legitimate Flowise custom tool/function nodes an operator intentionally uses to shell out
  • Ops staff debugging inside the Flowise container via a node REPL that spawns bash
  • Supervisor/PM2-style process managers restarting node via a shell
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("npm","yarn","node_modules/.bin","npm-lifecycle") or ParentCmd has_any ("npm","yarn","pm2"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host — confirm parent is the Flowise node service and inspect ChildCmd for reverse-shell flags (nc -e, /dev/tcp, bash -i) and the destination IP:port. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, kill the nc/sh PID, and block the outbound C2 IP/port at the egress firewall; snapshot the container for forensics. 3) Hunt: review Flowise access logs for POST /api/v1/document-store/loader/process and Upsert calls near the alert time, identify the authenticated user/API token, and search other hosts for node spawning shells.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs","node.js")
| where FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat","sh","bash","dash","ksh")
| where FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
      or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","/dev/tcp/","bash -i","0>&1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          Child = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat","sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
      or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","/dev/tcp/","bash -i","0>&1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reverse-shell egress from netcat/socat on Flowise host AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound network connections initiated by nc/ncat/netcat/socat (or a shell carrying reverse-shell flags) on the Flowise server — the command-and-control leg of the CVE-2026-69251 RCE where the payload connects back to attacker infrastructure (PoC used 172.17.0.1:1337). These tools have no legitimate role in a Flowise application container. Rationale: Targets the reverse-shell C2 described in the PoC (nc 172.17.0.1 1337 -e /bin/sh). Rather than hardcode the Docker-internal PoC IP, it flags any nc/socat egress or shell with reverse-shell flags — these binaries making outbound connections on a Flowise app host is high-signal. Sentinel left blank: ASIM ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-process attribution, so the same logic is covered by the ImProcessCreate execution UC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g32j-mmxr-gfq5 • https://www.cryptika.com/six-flowise-rce-flaws-let-attackers-execute-code-on-ai-workflow-servers/
ATT&CKT1571 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin using nc for a legitimate port/connectivity test from the host
  • socat used as a legitimate TCP relay/port-forward in a service's startup script
  • Monitoring or backup tooling that bundles netcat for health probes
  • Container network debugging (nc -z) during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-z ","-w ","port check","healthcheck") or RemoteIP startswith "127.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP/RemotePort and InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the reverse-shell shape (-e, /dev/tcp) and whether the destination is external/attacker-owned. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the nc/socat process, and block the destination IP:port at egress; capture memory/container snapshot. 3) Hunt: correlate to the parent Flowise node process, review who authenticated to Flowise and which chatflow/document-store was upserted, and sweep other Flowise hosts for the same egress binary.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat","socat")
      or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","/dev/tcp/","bash -i","0>&1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc

Malicious JavaScript entity file written into Flowise storage by node AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Flowise node process writing a .js file into the Flowise storage/home directory — the delivery step where an attacker uploads a JS payload via the Document Store File Loader (POST /api/v1/document-store/loader/process) that is later loaded as a TypeORM DataSource entity. Document stores normally hold PDFs/text, so a runtime-written .js blob is anomalous. Rationale: Uses the article's delivery artifact — a .js file (PoC filename rce.js, mime application/x-javascript) uploaded via the Document Store File Loader and persisted into Flowise's FILE-STORAGE/home path, then referenced as a TypeORM entity. A running node service writing executable .js into its document-store/storage tree is abnormal (normal ingest is PDF/text). Hunting tier because attacker-controlled filename and exact storage subpath vary. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g32j-mmxr-gfq5 • https://www.cryptika.com/six-flowise-rce-flaws-let-attackers-execute-code-on-ai-workflow-servers/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flowise application updates/rebuilds writing .js assets under its install path (should be outside the storage/.flowise data tree)
  • A developer legitimately ingesting source-code files into a document store for a code-QA chatflow
  • Flowise cache/temp .js files written during normal flow execution
  • Backup/restore jobs repopulating the .flowise storage directory
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "node_modules" and FolderPath !has "/dist/" and FolderPath !has "/build/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the written .js file and inspect its contents for RCE gadgets such as process.mainModule.require('child_process'), execSync, or reverse-shell strings; note the SHA256. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host if the payload is malicious, and revoke the Flowise session/API token of the uploading user. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for node spawning shells/nc referencing that path, and review document-store loader/upsert API calls to enumerate any other uploaded entity files.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where FileName endswith ".js"
| where FolderPath has_any ("flowise",".flowise","storage","document-store","uploads")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".js"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("flowise",".flowise","storage","document-store","uploads")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Keyv-Linked npm Worm Poisons Hundreds of Packages, Plants Claude Code and VS Code Hooks

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A credential-stealing npm worm that first appeared in keyv@6.0.0 spread beyond the Keyv and Cacheable namespaces into hundreds of packages across multiple organizations on August 4, 2026. SafeDep verified 353 poisoned versions across 79 package names in the npm registry. Its monitoring put the wider footprint at 442 versions across 353 names, while Aikido later reported at least 868 packages

npm preinstall lifecycle spawns 'node setup.mjs' / Math_Symbol.js (Shai-Hulud worm hook) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud 'Here We Go Again' worm's install-time execution: a poisoned npm package (keyv@6.0.0, flat-cache@6.1.23, cache-manager@7.2.9, etc.) declares `node setup.mjs` as its preinstall command and ships setup.mjs + Math_Symbol.js. Fires when node executes those exact staging files inside a package-install context on a dev workstation or CI runner. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim `node setup.mjs` preinstall command and the two published payload files (setup.mjs, Math_Symbol.js); Math_Symbol.js is a near-unique string with effectively zero benign use. Cross-checked against Socket, Aikido and Datadog Security Labs write-ups confirming setup.mjs is the preinstall stage-one. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/popular-npm-packages-in-the-keyv-and-cacheable-namespaces-compromised-in-active-supply-chain • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/keyv-and-friends-compromised-in-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate in-house package that genuinely ships a build helper literally named setup.mjs and runs it from a lifecycle script
  • Monorepo bootstrap tooling that invokes 'node setup.mjs' during 'npm ci' on CI runners
  • Developer manually running 'node setup.mjs' from an unrelated project of the same filename
  • Math_Symbol.js should almost never appear benignly — treat any hit on that token as high priority
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs" and FolderPath !contains "node_modules" and ProcessCommandLine !has "Math_Symbol.js" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("preinstall","npm ci","npm install"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full command line and parent chain; confirm the process worked out of a node_modules/<pkg> path and identify the resolved package + version from the install log or lockfile. Hash the setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js and compare to campaign SHA256s. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/runner and treat it as credential-exposed. Per SafeDep guidance, locate and remove the malware's token-revocation watcher BEFORE rotating any tokens (rotating first can trigger an attacker-supplied handler). 3) HUNT: Search for child Bun execution, contact to GitHub release downloads by node, and creation of .claude/.vscode hook files on the same host; audit npm/GitHub/cloud tokens resolvable from that machine for abuse.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","node","cmd.exe","sh","bash","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","npm install","npm ci","npm-cli.js","lifecycle")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node","cmd","bash","sh","pnpm","yarn")
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","npm install","npm ci","lifecycle")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Standalone Bun 1.3.13 runtime pulled/executed inside npm install chain (worm stage-two) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the worm's evasion step: setup.mjs downloads the Bun 1.3.13 runtime from GitHub and execFileSyncs it to run the compiled 727,680-byte credential-stealing bundle, keeping the stealer logic out of the preinstall file. Fires when a Bun process is spawned by node or from a setup.mjs context, or when node itself fetches a Bun release binary. Rationale: Uses the article's exact stage-two mechanic — setup.mjs fetching Bun 1.3.13 and execFileSync'ing it — corroborated by Upwind and Datadog which document Bun v1.3.13 downloaded from GitHub and invoked via execFileSync. Bun as a direct child of node is the anomalous pivot; standalone Bun is legit but node-spawning-Bun during install is not. Cross-checked against: • https://www.upwind.io/feed/mini-shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-worm • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Projects that legitimately use Bun as a task runner invoked from Node scripts (e.g. 'node' orchestrator calling 'bun run')
  • CI pipelines that install Bun via a Node-based setup action
  • Developers experimenting with Bun where a node process shells out to bun
  • Toolchains bundling bun as an optional dependency spawned by a node CLI
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "bun run" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js") and FolderPath has_any ("\\.bun\\","/.bun/"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Bun binary path (unexpected under a package/temp dir vs a user-installed ~/.bun) and inspect the parent node command line for setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js. Verify the Bun binary hash/version = 1.3.13. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host and block outbound from the Bun/node process; treat all locally-resolvable credentials as exposed. 3) HUNT: Look on the same host for a preceding 'node setup.mjs' preinstall event, GitHub release fetches of the Bun binary, credential-file access by node/bun, and creation of Shai-Hulud exfil artifacts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "bun"
| where ParentProcessName has "node" or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud plants Claude Code / VS Code auto-execution hook (setup.mjs in .claude or .vscode) AIInstallation High
Hunts the worm's second execution path: it writes .claude/settings.json (SessionStart hook), .vscode/tasks.json (Environment Setup task, runOn: folderOpen), and cross-referencing setup.mjs files into a repo's .claude and .vscode directories so the payload runs when a developer trusts the workspace. Fires on creation of setup.mjs (or the hook manifests) inside those config directories. Rationale: Anchors on the article's precise artifacts — .claude/settings.json SessionStart hook, .vscode/tasks.json runOn:folderOpen, and cross-referencing setup.mjs files in both dirs. A setup.mjs living inside .claude/ or .vscode/ is essentially never legitimate, making it a high-fidelity, worm-specific persistence signal confirmed by JFrog and Semgrep's April lightning-PyPI report of the same hooks. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again-mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-antv-ecosystem
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately keeps a workspace bootstrap script named setup.mjs — but placing it inside .vscode/.claude is unusual and worth review
  • Legit edits to .vscode/tasks.json or .claude/settings.json alone (query requires the setup.mjs pairing for high confidence)
  • Repo templating tools that scaffold .vscode automation tasks
  • IDE extensions writing their own settings.json (won't match the setup.mjs selection)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the dropped .claude/settings.json and .vscode/tasks.json — confirm the SessionStart hook / runOn:folderOpen task invokes setup.mjs, and read setup.mjs for the Bun-download stage. Identify the initiating process (git checkout vs node write). 2) CONTAIN: Quarantine the repo/workspace, revoke workspace trust, and block the host from opening it in VS Code/Claude Code until cleaned; treat the host as credential-exposed if the hook already fired. 3) HUNT: Search version control for the planting commit (author github-actions[bot] / claude@users.noreply.github.com), and check other cloned repos on the fleet for the same .claude/.vscode hook files.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has "\\.claude\\" or FolderPath has "/.claude/" or FolderPath has "\\.vscode\\" or FolderPath has "/.vscode/")
| where FileName =~ "setup.mjs"
   or (FileName =~ "settings.json" and (FolderPath has "\\.claude\\" or FolderPath has "/.claude/"))
   or (FileName =~ "tasks.json" and (FolderPath has "\\.vscode\\" or FolderPath has "/.vscode/"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (TargetFilePath has "\\.claude\\" or TargetFilePath has "/.claude/" or TargetFilePath has "\\.vscode\\" or TargetFilePath has "/.vscode/")
| where TargetFileName =~ "setup.mjs"
   or (TargetFileName =~ "settings.json" and TargetFilePath has ".claude")
   or (TargetFileName =~ "tasks.json" and TargetFilePath has ".vscode")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node/Bun reads developer & cloud credential stores during npm activity (worm harvest) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-harvesting core of the bundle, which collects GitHub, npm, cloud, Vault, Kubernetes, database and private-key material. Fires when a node or bun process touches high-value credential stores (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.kube/config, .vault-token, .git-credentials, gh hosts, SSH private keys) — access patterns a JS runtime rarely performs benignly. Rationale: Maps the article's explicit harvest list (GitHub, npm, cloud, Vault, Kubernetes, DB, private-key) to the concrete on-disk stores a JS runtime would read; Falcon FileOpenInfo captures the read directly, while Defender/Sentinel catch node/bun-initiated file events on those paths. Datadog left empty because the listed linux.auditd schema exposes no file-path attribute to filter on. .npmrc deliberately excluded (npm reads it normally). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit node CLIs built on the AWS SDK reading ~/.aws/credentials (e.g. serverless/CDK tooling)
  • kubectl-adjacent node tooling reading ~/.kube/config
  • Node-based git helpers reading .git-credentials
  • Developer scripts that load SSH keys for programmatic git over a node process
  • gh-cli wrapper tools reading ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws","cdk","serverless","kubectl","gh ") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Correlate the credential access with a preceding 'node setup.mjs' / Bun execution on the same host in the same window; if present, escalate immediately. Enumerate exactly which credential stores were touched. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/runner. Remove the token-revocation watcher first (per SafeDep), then rotate every credential resolvable from that machine — npm, GitHub, cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure), Vault, kube, DB and SSH keys — and invalidate active sessions. 3) HUNT: Check for outbound exfil, creation of a 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again' GitHub repo under stolen tokens, and unexpected npm publish events from the compromised identity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
| where (FolderPath has "\\.aws\\" or FolderPath has "/.aws/" or FolderPath has "\\.kube\\" or FolderPath has "/.kube/" or FolderPath has "\\.config\\gh\\" or FolderPath has "/.config/gh/")
   or FileName in~ (".git-credentials",".vault-token","id_rsa","id_ed25519",".netrc")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.aws/credentials","\\.aws\\credentials","/.kube/config","\\.kube\\config",".vault-token",".git-credentials","/.config/gh/hosts.yml","id_rsa","id_ed25519",".netrc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Node or Bun Accesses Cloud and Developer Credential Stores (Shai-Hulud harvest)
id: 3f8b6d21-4a90-4e57-bc12-7c1e9d0a5f33

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake Adobe and Zoom Updates Install ScreenConnect for Persistent Remote Access

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 18 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an active, multi-wave campaign that employs social engineering lures themed around Adobe and Zoom software updates, business document reviews, and system maintenance utilities to stealthily deploy Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) programs like ConnectWise ScreenConnect. The campaign has been codenamed SMOKE#SCREEN by Securonix Threat

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Powercat fake Xeno loader chain (xeno.exe → AppData javaw.exe → decompiler.exe) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake Adobe and Zoom Updates Install ScreenConnect for Persistent Remote Access
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SMOKE#SCREEN security-product registry tamper (SmartScreen/Defender) by script host · [LLM] SMOKE#SCREEN silent msiexec install of ScreenConnect / ConnectWise Control · [LLM] Powercat stage-3 persistence via HKCU Run 'Display Calibration' → GameDVR payload · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SMOKE#SCREEN ScreenConnect relay C2 beacon to attacker IPs / port 8041 · [LLM] SMOKE#SCREEN Cloudflare Quick Tunnel C2 (trycloudflare.com staging subdomain) · [LLM] Powercat stage-2 C2 to solthere.net redeem endpoint · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
SMOKE#SCREEN ScreenConnect relay C2 beacon to attacker IPs / port 8041 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the SMOKE#SCREEN staging/relay infrastructure (WsgiDAV stager 207.174.0.143, C# stager 207.189.11.170, and corroborated relay clusters 188.214.34.20 / 169.40.2.68) and ScreenConnect default relay port 8041. This is the persistence-C2 tail of the fake Adobe/Zoom update chain. Rationale: Uses the article's WsgiDAV stager IP (207.174.0.143), the C# payload host (207.189.11.170) and the ScreenConnect relay port 8041; the two additional relay IPs and the port were confirmed by the GuardianMSSP and SC Media re-analysis of the same Securonix report, so they meet the second-source bar. Cross-checked against: • https://www.guardianmssp.com/2026/08/04/fake-adobe-and-zoom-updates-install-screenconnect-for-persistent-remote-access/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/fake-interactive-zoom-call-leads-to-malicious-screenconnect-download • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/memory-loader-drops-screenconnect
ATT&CKT1219 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organization legitimately runs ConnectWise ScreenConnect on the default relay port 8041 to its own on-prem/cloud relay
  • Security researcher or SOC sandbox intentionally detonating the sample and beaconing to the IOCs
  • Proxy/NAT egress where an internal appliance uses port 8041 for an unrelated service
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment pods that actively probe the IOC IPs
Suppression filter
and not (RemotePort == 8041 and RemoteUrl endswith "<your-managed-screenconnect-relay-fqdn>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which internal host initiated the flow and the initiating process; a ScreenConnect client with a relay you do not manage on 8041 is confirmation. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the four IOC IPs and port 8041 to untrusted destinations at the egress firewall, and kill/uninstall the unmanaged ScreenConnect client. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the msiexec silent-install chain (UC4), SmartScreen/Defender registry tamper (UC2), and cloudflared tunnel activity (UC3).

SMOKE#SCREEN security-product registry tamper (SmartScreen/Defender) by script host AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the batch loader stage that disables SmartScreen and Defender real-time protection via registry edits before running the staged MSI. Scoped to script/console interpreters writing the specific security keys, matching the campaign's nine-step Defender-destruction sequence. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit 'disable AMSI / turn off SmartScreen via Registry / nine-step Defender destruction' step by scoping the exact SmartScreen and Defender RTP value writes to script/console interpreters run by non-machine accounts. Falcon left blank: these non-ASEP registry writes are not covered by the AsepValueUpdate event in the FDR reference. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/news/fake-interactive-zoom-call-leads-to-malicious-screenconnect-download
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin or GPO troubleshooting temporarily disabling SmartScreen on a test host
  • EDR migration project scripting Defender RTP off before installing a third-party AV
  • Software packaging/imaging pipelines that disable SmartScreen for silent installs
  • Legitimate MDM/Intune scripts toggling these keys via powershell
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("CcmExec.exe","IntuneManagementExtension.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "MpPreference -Disable"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine — a one-liner from cmd/wscript that also disables multiple protections in sequence (SmartScreen + Defender RTP) is high-confidence; a lone GPO-driven change is likely benign. 2) Contain: re-enable the protections, isolate the host, and capture the parent script for analysis. 3) Hunt: look on the same host for a Zone.Identifier-stripped MSI, silent msiexec ScreenConnect install (UC4), and relay beacons (UC1).
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "SmartScreenEnabled" and RegistryValueData =~ "Off")
     or (RegistryValueName =~ "EnableSmartScreen" and RegistryValueData == "0")
     or (RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection" and RegistryValueName in~ ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable","DisableOnAccessProtection") and RegistryValueData == "1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","reg.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (RegistryValue =~ "SmartScreenEnabled" and RegistryValueData =~ "Off")
     or (RegistryValue =~ "EnableSmartScreen" and RegistryValueData == "0")
     or (RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection" and RegistryValue in~ ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable") and RegistryValueData == "1")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","reg.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SMOKE#SCREEN Cloudflare Quick Tunnel C2 (trycloudflare.com staging subdomain) AICommand & Control High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network activity to the SMOKE#SCREEN Cloudflare Quick Tunnel used by MemoryLoader.cs (subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare.com) and, more broadly, first-party non-browser processes reaching any *.trycloudflare.com ephemeral tunnel. Rationale: The exact tunnel subdomain (subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare.com) is a hard IOC named in the article and the staging server was confirmed to run cloudflared.exe; the broader clause flags first-time non-browser egress to trycloudflare.com without blanket-allowlisting the CDN. Zscaler's MemoryLoader write-up independently confirms the Quick Tunnel usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/memory-loader-drops-screenconnect • https://www.guardianmssp.com/2026/08/04/fake-adobe-and-zoom-updates-install-screenconnect-for-persistent-remote-access/
ATT&CKT1572 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using Cloudflare Tunnel / cloudflared to expose a local dev service
  • A user visiting a benign site hosted behind a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel in a browser
  • Security testing of trycloudflare tunnels by internal red team
  • IT using trycloudflare for temporary remote support demos
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cloudflared.exe") and RemoteUrl has "subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: the exact subdomain is a direct hit — treat as confirmed; for generic *.trycloudflare.com, check the initiating process (a non-browser like a .NET loader, wscript, or an MSI-dropped binary is high-signal). 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy, isolate the host, and capture the initiating binary (likely the MemoryLoader .NET stager). 3) Hunt: correlate with cloudflared.exe execution, the ScreenConnect relay beacon (UC1), and the silent MSI install (UC4) on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare.com"
    or (RemoteUrl endswith "trycloudflare.com" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","cloudflared.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has "trycloudflare.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SMOKE#SCREEN silent msiexec install of ScreenConnect / ConnectWise Control AIInstallation Medium
Hunts msiexec.exe launched with silent flags (/quiet, /qn, /passive) that spawns a ScreenConnect/ConnectWise Control client binary — the RMM-abuse install step common to every SMOKE#SCREEN lure once the MSI's Zone.Identifier ADS is stripped. Rationale: Encodes the corroborated 'msiexec /quiet or /passive followed by ScreenConnect binary execution' behaviour, keyed on the ConnectWise product/company version metadata so renamed binaries still match. Kept at hunting tier because managed RMM deployments use the same shape — pair with the unknown-relay context from UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://www.guardianmssp.com/2026/08/04/fake-adobe-and-zoom-updates-install-screenconnect-for-persistent-remote-access/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/fake-interactive-zoom-call-leads-to-malicious-screenconnect-download
ATT&CKT1219 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT deploying ScreenConnect/ConnectWise agents silently via RMM or SCCM
  • MSP onboarding a managed endpoint with the sanctioned relay
  • Software-packaging test lab installing ConnectWise for evaluation
  • Self-service ScreenConnect reinstall by an authorized support technician
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "<your-sanctioned-screenconnect-instance-id>"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the ScreenConnect relay/instance from the installed config and compare to your sanctioned relay allowlist — an unknown relay (esp. on 8041 to UC1 IPs) confirms malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, uninstall the unmanaged agent, block the relay. 3) Hunt: look for the preceding SmartScreen/Defender tamper (UC2), Zone.Identifier removal on the source MSI, and the delivery lure (Dropbox/trycloudflare, UC3).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/quiet","/qn","/passive")
| where FileName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl")
     or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWise Control")
     or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ConnectWise"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has "msiexec.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("/quiet","/qn","/passive")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ScreenConnect","ConnectWiseControl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Powercat fake Xeno loader chain (xeno.exe → AppData javaw.exe → decompiler.exe) AIDelivery High
Hunts the Bitdefender/ThreatLocker-tracked Powercat infection chain delivered via fake Xeno Roblox executor: a xeno.exe first stage that extracts a bundled JRE and runs javaw.exe from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin, then launches an Allatori-obfuscated JAR masquerading as decompiler.exe. Rationale: Uses the article's named stages (xeno.exe, decompiler.exe) plus the Bitdefender/BleepingComputer-confirmed bundled-JRE path %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin\javaw.exe; a decompiler.exe that is actually a JAR and a Java runtime under a user AppData path are both strongly anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-roblox-xeno-script-launcher-pushes-infostealer-rat-malware/ • https://www.threatlocker.com/blog/powercat-malware-campaign-fake-game-cheats-deliver-infostealer-targeting-discord-roblox-and-crypto-wallets
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer with a portable/embedded JRE under AppData running javaw.exe for a legitimate tool
  • A build/CI tool named decompiler.exe used by reverse-engineering staff
  • Minecraft/modding launchers that bundle their own JRE in AppData
  • Portable Java IDE plugins launched from a user profile
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("minecraftlauncher.exe","javaw.exe") and FolderPath has @"\.minecraft\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the javaw.exe path is %LOCALAPPDATA%\Java\jre\bin and check for a sibling XenoIcon.jpg (key file) and decompiler.exe JAR; hash the parent xeno.exe. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the java processes, and remove the AppData\Java staging and the GameDVR payload directory. 3) Hunt: pivot to solthere.net C2 (UC6) and the 'Display Calibration' Run-key persistence (UC7), then scope credential/wallet-theft on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "javaw.exe" and FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Java\jre\bin\")
     or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "xeno.exe"
     or FileName =~ "decompiler.exe"
     or (FileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "decompiler")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "javaw.exe" and ActingProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\Java\jre\bin\")
     or ParentProcessName has "xeno.exe"
     or ActingProcessName has "decompiler.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Powercat stage-2 C2 to solthere.net redeem endpoint AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS/network activity to the Powercat stage-2 command-and-control domain solthere.net (observed path /api/v1/redeem for pulling the next-stage payload with an AES+Base64 key). Any internal host resolving this domain is a strong Powercat indicator. Rationale: solthere.net is the article's named Powercat C2 domain, independently confirmed by Bitdefender (redeem endpoint /api/v1/redeem) and BleepingComputer; a bare domain match on a rarely-benign infrastructure name is high-fidelity and alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/fake-xeno-roblox-discord-executor • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-roblox-xeno-script-launcher-pushes-infostealer-rat-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox or analyst VM detonating the sample and resolving the C2
  • Security scanner/crawler pre-fetching IOC domains for enrichment
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS logging a blocked lookup (still worth reviewing)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and initiating process — javaw.exe from an AppData JRE (UC5) confirms Powercat. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block solthere.net at protective DNS, isolate the host, and terminate the java stealer processes. 3) Hunt: check for the 'Display Calibration' Run key (UC7), the GameDVR payload directory, and browser/wallet/Discord credential access indicative of stage-3 theft.
