Safe Links click resolving through a cloud-PaaS redirect chain into AitM phishing AIDelivery Medium
Hunts UrlClickEvents where the resolved redirect chain (UrlChain) or final URL lands on one of the campaign's abused PaaS platforms — mirroring the article's Stage 1→2 flow of compromised-site CAPTCHA relay bouncing the victim to a *.workers.dev Ultraviolet proxy page. Targets the redirect landing, not the innocuous-looking link in the email body. Rationale: Anchors on the article's multi-stage redirect (email link -> compromised site CAPTCHA -> *.workers.dev), so it inspects the Safe Links UrlChain rather than the benign first-hop domain. ClickedThrough is the high-fidelity user-bypass signal. PaaS suffixes taken directly from the article's platform table. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://urlscan.io/blog/2026/04/15/ProxyingTrust/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1583.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit newsletter/marketing tracking link that happens to redirect through a Vercel/Netlify edge function
  • Internal app or CI notification linking to a github.io or pages.dev docs page
  • A vendor's URL-shortener whose final hop is a serverless health page
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platforms hosting lures on PaaS
  • Web3 wallet flows resolving through a dweb.link IPFS gateway
Suppression filter
| where IsClickedThrough == true or Workload == "Email"
Response runbook
1) Triage: detonate the full UrlChain terminal URL; confirm a Microsoft login iframe/BitB window and check whether the redirect emerged from a compromised legitimate first-hop domain. Confirm ActionType/IsClickedThrough (user actually reached the page). 2) Contain: quarantine/soft-delete the source message tenant-wide via EmailPostDeliveryEvents ZAP, block the terminal FQDN, force credential reset + session revocation for the clicker. 3) Hunt: enumerate other recipients of the same NetworkMessageId/sender, and pivot each clicker into UC-3 to catch AitM session replay.
let PaaS = dynamic(["workers.dev","pages.dev","vercel.app","github.io","netlify.app","dweb.link"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend Chain = tostring(UrlChain)
| where Chain has_any (PaaS) or Url has_any (PaaS)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, UrlChain=Chain, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, IPAddress, Workload, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let PaaS = dynamic(["workers.dev","pages.dev","vercel.app","github.io","netlify.app","dweb.link"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend Chain = tostring(UrlChain)
| where Chain has_any (PaaS) or Url has_any (PaaS)
| project TimeGenerated, AccountUpn, Url, UrlChain=Chain, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, IPAddress, Workload, NetworkMessageId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
AitM session hijack: PaaS phishing-page visit followed by successful Entra sign-in from a different IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates an endpoint browser connecting to a campaign PaaS domain (Stage 2/3 Ultraviolet proxy + BitB) with a successful, MFA-satisfied Entra sign-in for the same user within 30 minutes whose source IP does NOT match the victim's device — the hallmark of the attacker replaying the intercepted session token from their own infrastructure. This is the payoff step the article describes: credentials and MFA relayed, then the attacker holds a live session. Rationale: Expresses the article's core AitM outcome: MFA relayed through the *.workers.dev Ultraviolet proxy, then the attacker uses the token from their own IP. The IP-mismatch clause (sign-in source != victim device public IP) within a 30-min window of the PaaS visit is the discriminator corroborated by Cofense/Securelist noting the token is replayed from a different IP/ASN than where the victim authenticated. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/cloud-platforms-in-phishing/120832/ • https://cofense.com/blog/how-cloudflare-services-are-abused-for-credential-theft-and-malware-distribution • https://ringsafe.in/cloudflare-fronted-phishing-in-2026-how-workers-pages-tunnels-and-r2-became-default-phishing-infrastructure/
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1111 T1550.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User visits a legit PaaS-hosted app then signs in to M365 over corporate VPN/egress with a different public IP than the device reports
  • Roaming/mobile user whose device PublicIP and sign-in IP legitimately differ (cellular vs Wi-Fi)
  • CDN/proxy egress that rewrites the outbound IP for O365 traffic
  • Shared-device/kiosk scenarios where DeviceInfo PublicIP is stale
  • Developer testing their own Cloudflare Worker while authenticated to Azure
Suppression filter
| where SignInIP !in (dynamic([])) and Country != ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the sign-in IP is a hosting/datacenter ASN (not corporate egress or the user's ISP) and that the PaaS URL detonates to a Microsoft login/BitB page — that combination is a confirmed token theft. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens/sessions for the account (Entra 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-registration of MFA; block the SignInIP and PaaS FQDN. 3) Hunt: review AuditLogs/CloudAppEvents for attacker-created inbox forwarding rules, new OAuth app consents, MFA method additions, and mailbox exfiltration under that account after the sign-in time.
let Window = 30m;
let PhishConns = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe")
    | where RemoteUrl endswith ".workers.dev" or RemoteUrl endswith ".pages.dev" or RemoteUrl endswith ".vercel.app" or RemoteUrl endswith ".github.io" or RemoteUrl endswith ".netlify.app" or RemoteUrl endswith ".dweb.link"
    | where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountUpn)
    | project ConnTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, PhishUrl=RemoteUrl, UserUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn;
let DevIP = DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, PublicIP) by DeviceName;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project SignInTime=Timestamp, AccountUpn, SignInIP=IPAddress, Application, Country, City
| join kind=inner PhishConns on $left.AccountUpn == $right.UserUpn
| where SignInTime between (ConnTime .. ConnTime + Window)
| join kind=leftouter DevIP on DeviceName
| where isempty(PublicIP) or SignInIP != PublicIP
| project SignInTime, ConnTime, DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ConnTime), AccountUpn, DeviceName, PhishUrl, SignInIP, DevicePublicIP=PublicIP, Application, Country, City
| order by SignInTime desc
let Window = 30m;
let Phish = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DstHostname endswith ".workers.dev" or DstHostname endswith ".pages.dev" or DstHostname endswith ".vercel.app" or DstHostname endswith ".github.io" or DstHostname endswith ".netlify.app" or DstHostname endswith ".dweb.link"
    | where isnotempty(SrcUsername)
    | project ConnTime=TimeGenerated, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr, PhishHost=DstHostname;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| project SignInTime=TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SignInIP=IPAddress, AppDisplayName, Location
| join kind=inner Phish on $left.UserPrincipalName == $right.SrcUsername
| where SignInTime between (ConnTime .. ConnTime + Window)
| where SignInIP != SrcIpAddr
| project SignInTime, ConnTime, DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ConnTime), UserPrincipalName, PhishHost, SignInIP, VictimIP=SrcIpAddr, AppDisplayName, Location
| order by SignInTime desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

Google Deletes 3 ADK AI Workflows After Malicious GitHub Issue Could Trigger Privileged Agent

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 7 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Google deleted three AI agent workflows from its Agent Development Kit (ADK) Python repository. Pillar Security showed that a public GitHub issue could manipulate a triage agent into triggering a privileged code-fixing agent. The researchers said the public agent could be prompt-injected into posting /adk-issue-fix as adk-bot. They identified the bot as a collaborator, so that comment satisfied

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1566 T1566.002

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Git spawning shell/interpreter from runner temp dir (hook payload execution) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Git core.hooksPath redirected to writable temp dir on CI runner (ADK allowlist bypass)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Git core.hooksPath redirected to writable temp dir on CI runner (ADK allowlist bypass) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the exact code-execution primitive Pillar Security demonstrated against Google's ADK issue-fix workflow: the command allowlist only permitted commands whose first token was gh or git, so the agent wrote a payload and abused `git -c core.hooksPath=<dir>` / `git config core.hooksPath` to make an allowed Git invocation execute attacker-controlled code via a custom hook path. Fires when git is run with core.hooksPath pointing at a runner-writable location. Rationale: Anchors on the exact bypass the article/Pillar describe verbatim ('core.hooksPath can redirect Git to another directory', 'make an allowed Git command execute it through a custom hook path') combined with GitHub-Actions runner-writable paths (/home/runner, /runner/_work, _actions) so it fires on the CI-runner exploitation, not on dev laptops. The .husky exclusion strips the one common legitimate core.hooksPath user. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-deletes-3-adk-ai-workflows-after.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4204906/google-adk-flaws-reveal-what-happens-when-ai-agents-trust-the-wrong-message.html • https://www.scworld.com/news/researchers-find-agent-to-agent-privilege-escalation-in-googles-adk-for-python-repo • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/08/03/google-dev-kit-spurs-first-ever-agent-on-agent-violence/5282496
ATT&CKT1574 T1059.004 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Husky/pre-commit dev tooling setting core.hooksPath to a repo-relative .husky directory (excluded by filter)
  • A CI pipeline that legitimately installs a shared hooks directory under the workspace via git config core.hooksPath
  • Developer running git with an explicit --config core.hooksPath while debugging hooks locally on a self-hosted runner
  • Monorepo bootstrap scripts that point core.hooksPath at a vendored tools directory under _work
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has ".husky" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"core\.hooksPath=(\.|\./|/[^ ]*/repo)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full git command line and the initiating process — confirm the core.hooksPath value points at a writable/temp path and inspect the referenced hooks directory for a freshly-written executable (pre-commit/post-checkout/post-commit). Correlate the runner, workflow run, and triggering issue/PR number. 2) Contain: pause the self-hosted runner and revoke/rotate any PAT, GOOGLE_API_KEY, and GCP service-account key exposed to that job; invalidate the runner's registration token. 3) Hunt: on the same host/AID look for outbound connections from git/curl/python to non-github.com/non-googleapis.com hosts (token exfil), and review recent bot-authored PRs/branches for injected code.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "git"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "core.hooksPath"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/home/runner/","/runner/_work","_actions")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has ".husky"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "git" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "git "
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "core.hooksPath"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/home/runner/","/runner/_work","_actions")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has ".husky"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Git core.hooksPath Redirected to Writable Runner Directory (ADK CI Abuse)
id: 8f2e1c4a-6b3d-4a1e-9c7f-2d5b8e0a1f34
description: Detects git invoked with core.hooksPath pointing at a runner-writable temp directory, the allowlist-bypass code-execution technique in the Pillar Security ADK issue-fix workflow report.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-deletes-3-adk-ai-workflows-after.html
  - https://www.pillar.security/blog/my-agentic-trust-issues-from-prompt-injection-to-supply-chain-compromise-on-gemini-cli
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1574
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '/git'
  selection_hooks:
    CommandLine|contains: 'core.hooksPath'
  selection_paths:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/var/tmp/'
      - '/dev/shm/'
      - '/home/runner/'
      - '/runner/_work'
      - '_actions'
  filter_husky:
    CommandLine|contains: '.husky'
  condition: selection_img and selection_hooks and selection_paths and not filter_husky
level: medium
source:(linux.auditd OR linux.syslog OR linux.sysmon) @process.name:git @process.command_line:*core.hooksPath* (@process.command_line:*/tmp/* OR @process.command_line:*/var/tmp/* OR @process.command_line:*/dev/shm/* OR @process.command_line:*/home/runner/* OR @process.command_line:*/runner/_work*) -@process.command_line:*.husky*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/git$/i
| CommandLine=/core\.hooksPath/i
| CommandLine=/(\/tmp\/|\/var\/tmp\/|\/dev\/shm\/|\/home\/runner\/|\/runner\/_work|_actions)/i
| NOT (CommandLine=/\.husky/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=git Processes.process="*core.hooksPath*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| search (process="*/tmp/*" OR process="*/var/tmp/*" OR process="*/dev/shm/*" OR process="*/home/runner/*" OR process="*/runner/_work*" OR process="*_actions*")
| search NOT process="*.husky*"
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=git Processes.process="*core.hooksPath*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| search (process="*/tmp/*" OR process="*/var/tmp/*" OR process="*/dev/shm/*" OR process="*/home/runner/*" OR process="*/runner/_work*" OR process="*_actions*")
| search NOT process="*.husky*"
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Git spawning shell/interpreter from runner temp dir (hook payload execution) AIExploitation Medium
Complements the cmdline hunt by catching the payload actually running: once core.hooksPath is redirected, an 'allowed' git command executes the attacker's hook, so git becomes the parent of a shell/interpreter/downloader launched from a runner-writable path. On a CI runner git rarely spawns bash/python/curl, making the parent=git → interpreter-from-temp pairing high-signal. Rationale: Targets a different pivot than UC1 — the parent/child image relationship rather than a cmdline arg — catching the moment the redirected hook payload runs ('write a payload and make an allowed Git command execute it'). git parenting an interpreter from /runner/_work or /tmp on a self-hosted runner is inherently abnormal, giving high fidelity even without the core.hooksPath string in view. Datadog left empty: the listed linux.auditd schema exposes no parent-process field, so the parent=git → child pairing cannot be expressed there. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-deletes-3-adk-ai-workflows-after.html • https://www.pillar.security/blog/my-agentic-trust-issues-from-prompt-injection-to-supply-chain-compromise-on-gemini-cli • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/08/03/google-dev-kit-spurs-first-ever-agent-on-agent-violence/5282496
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1574
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate git hooks (pre-commit/post-checkout) implemented as shell/python scripts running during a normal CI checkout
  • Husky-managed hooks invoking node from the repo tree
  • Build tooling where git-lfs or a credential helper shells out to a helper script under the workspace
  • Repo bootstrap that runs a setup shell script via a post-merge hook on the runner
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has ".husky" or FolderPath has "/hooks/" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "core.hooksPath")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and script path — determine whether the interpreter is executing a file inside a hooks directory or an unexpected temp path, and whether the git parent used a redirected core.hooksPath (join to UC1 on the same host/time). Identify the workflow run and triggering PR/issue. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, kill the process tree, and rotate every credential the job held (bot PAT, GOOGLE_API_KEY, GCP SA key). 3) Hunt: review outbound traffic from the child process for credential exfiltration to non-GitHub/Google hosts, and check for bot-created forks/branches or PRs opened around the same timestamp.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "git"
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","python","python3","perl","node","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/home/runner/","/runner/_work"))
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/runner/_work"))
    or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "core.hooksPath")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "git"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","python","python3","perl","node","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/home/runner/","/runner/_work"))
    or (ParentProcessCommandLine has "core.hooksPath")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Keyv and friends compromised in active Shai-Hulud supply chain attack
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm preinstall hook executing node setup.mjs (Shai-Hulud dropper) · [LLM] Shai-Hulud payload files setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js written into node_modules · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Bun runtime fetched from oven-sh GitHub releases during npm install
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Bun runtime executing Shai-Hulud Math_Symbol.js credential stealer · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
npm preinstall hook executing node setup.mjs (Shai-Hulud dropper) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud supply-chain worm's execution stage: a poisoned npm package's 'preinstall':'node setup.mjs' lifecycle hook auto-running the obfuscated dropper the moment a developer runs npm install. Anchored on node.exe launching a script literally named setup.mjs under a package manager parent, which is not a normal legitimate pattern. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact preinstall payload string 'node setup.mjs'; setup.mjs is a non-standard filename and pairing node.exe + this script + a package-manager parent is a high-fidelity, article-specific signature confirmed by Datadog and Unit42 write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-detection/shai-hulud-worm/
ATT&CKT1204.003 T1546.016 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal package that genuinely ships a benign preinstall script named setup.mjs (rare but possible in monorepos)
  • Developer intentionally running a project's own setup.mjs build helper via node outside npm
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox for analysis
  • CI build agent installing a pinned pre-compromise version whose setup.mjs is a coincidental name
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("lifecycle","run-script") and FolderPath !has "node_modules")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and the enclosing node_modules package path; identify which npm package owns setup.mjs and its version, and check whether it is in the compromised list (keyv, cacheable, flat-cache, file-entry-cache, cache-manager, etc.). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill node/bun processes, and immediately rotate any credentials reachable from that dev machine — npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS keys, VAULT_TOKEN. 3) Hunt: search the org for any install of affected package versions, look for child bun.exe execution of Math_Symbol.js and outbound requests to oven-sh/bun releases, and review npm/GitHub audit logs for publishes made with the machine's tokens.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm-cli.js","cmd.exe","sh","bash","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node.exe","yarn","pnpm","cmd.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud payload files setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js written into node_modules AIInstallation High
Hunts the worm's install-stage artifacts: the two new files (setup.mjs dropper and Math_Symbol.js credential-stealer) being written inside a node_modules package directory. Every compromised package in the keyv family gained exactly these two filenames, making them a reliable on-disk indicator. Rationale: Uses the article's two exact dropped filenames (setup.mjs, Math_Symbol.js) constrained to node_modules; both are verbatim from the compromise and cross-confirmed as Shai-Hulud artifacts, giving an extremely low-FP on-disk indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign package coincidentally naming a build helper setup.mjs inside its published tarball
  • Local developer git-cloning the compromised repo for analysis (files land on disk without npm install)
  • Backup/AV quarantine tooling re-writing the file path during scanning
  • Monorepo tooling copying package fixtures containing a same-named test file
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the containing package.json to get the package name and version and hash setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js; confirm the version matches a known-poisoned release. 2) Contain: quarantine the files, isolate the host, and delete the affected node_modules; block the package version in the internal registry/proxy. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints and CI runners for the same two filenames, check whether Math_Symbol.js was executed (bun child process), and rotate every credential class the payload targets (npm, GitHub, AWS, Vault).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup.mjs","Math_Symbol.js")
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime fetched from oven-sh GitHub releases during npm install AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the worm's C2/staging step: setup.mjs silently downloading the Bun runtime from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/ so it can execute the payload with a runtime other than the local Node. Flags outbound requests to that release path originating from a node/npm/bun process tree. Rationale: Uses the article's exact staging URL path (github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/) tied to a node/npm/bun parent process; a package install that pulls the Bun runtime mid-install is anomalous and specific to this worm. Datadog Sysmon netflow lacks URL paths so that field and Sigma are omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-detection/shai-hulud-worm/
ATT&CKT1105 T1620 T1102
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI job that legitimately installs Bun as a project runtime/tool
  • Corporate mirror or artifact proxy pre-caching Bun releases
  • Docker base-image builds that fetch Bun as a documented dependency
  • Engineer manually evaluating Bun on their workstation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun upgrade","install bun","setup-bun"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and whether the Bun fetch coincided with an npm install and a setup.mjs execution on the same host within seconds. 2) Contain: if correlated with setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js, isolate the host, terminate bun/node, and rotate exposed credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for bun.exe executing Math_Symbol.js and for outbound HTTP to a Vault endpoint (the payload's Vault token fallback), and review which package version triggered the download.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","bun.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession

| where Url has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/\\bun(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*oven-sh/bun/releases/download*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.app Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Bun runtime executing Shai-Hulud Math_Symbol.js credential stealer AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access stage: the freshly downloaded Bun runtime executing Math_Symbol.js, the payload that harvests npm tokens from .npmrc, GitHub CLI tokens, AWS keys from ~/.aws/credentials, and the VAULT_TOKEN env var. Using Bun rather than the local Node is a defense-evasion tell, and the script name is verbatim from the campaign. Rationale: Combines the article's exact payload filename (Math_Symbol.js) with its exact evasion runtime (bun); Bun executing a package-dropped JS credential extractor is a near-zero-legitimate pattern and is the direct credential-access step described in the writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-detection/shai-hulud-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.005 T1528 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project genuinely running a script named Math_Symbol.js via Bun (extremely unlikely, but possible in a math/symbol-processing library)
  • Malware analyst detonating the payload with Bun in a lab
  • A red-team emulation of the Shai-Hulud chain during an authorized exercise
  • Security tooling replaying the sample for signature testing
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm bun.exe launched Math_Symbol.js and capture the parent chain (npm install -> node setup.mjs -> bun); collect the package name/version. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately and treat all locally reachable secrets as compromised — force-rotate npm tokens, GitHub PATs/session/OIDC tokens, AWS access keys and session tokens, and the Vault token; revoke active sessions. 3) Hunt: check npm and GitHub audit logs for publishes or repo pushes made with the stolen tokens (worm self-propagation), review AWS CloudTrail for use of the leaked keys, and sweep other dev hosts/CI runners for the same bun+Math_Symbol.js execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Math_Symbol.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bun.exe"
| where CommandLine has "Math_Symbol.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

DOUBLECUP Uses ClickFix and Cached PNGs to Deliver CountLoader and DeviceManager RAT

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 17 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A new Russian loader-as-a-service (LaaS) codenamed DOUBLECUP has been using ClickFix lures as a way to stage malware-laced PNG images in victims' browser cache and ultimately deliver CountLoader and a previously undocumented remote access trojan called DeviceManager. "The first stage drops a steganographic PNG image into the browser's cache, retrieves its hidden content, and executes the second

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] DOUBLECUP ClickFix: script interpreter reads steganographic PNG from browser cache · [LLM] DOUBLECUP delivery domain and /api/config endpoint contact · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] DeviceManager RAT: embedded Python spawned from Inno Setup installer in user space · [LLM] DeviceManager anti-analysis self-deletion: python spawns cmd rmdir + schtasks /delete · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DOUBLECUP / CountLoader / DeviceManager C2 IP connections · [LLM] DeviceManager EtherHiding: non-browser process resolving C2 via blockchain RPC · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
DOUBLECUP ClickFix: script interpreter reads steganographic PNG from browser cache AIDelivery High
Hunts the DOUBLECUP first-stage where a ClickFix-pasted command launches PowerShell/mshta/wscript/cscript whose command line references a browser cache directory AND a .png file, then extracts hidden JS/VBScript/PowerShell from the cached image. This is the article's core delivery signature and is independent of the (unreliable) parent process because ClickFix runs via the Win+R Run dialog. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit chain: ClickFix command 'searches the browser cache for the PNG image and extracts from it malicious JavaScript, VBScript, or PowerShell'. Pairing a script interpreter + a browser cache path + .png is high-fidelity and rarely legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-doublecup-clickfix-service-hides-malware-in-browser-cache-images/ • https://www.cynet.com/blog/clickfix-reloaded-from-mass-hijackloader-infections-to-stealth-etherhiding-rats/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browser dev/automation tooling (Puppeteer/Selenium) purging or reading cache2/Cache_Data during test runs
  • Endpoint cleanup utilities (CCleaner-style scripts) deleting .png thumbnails from browser cache folders
  • Enterprise browser-profile migration scripts copying cached assets including images
  • Security-tooling that carves and inspects browser cache artifacts for forensics
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccleaner.exe","chromedriver.exe","geckodriver.exe","node.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "Remove-Item"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent chain; ClickFix typically shows explorer.exe (Run dialog) as parent and a base64/IEX or Invoke-WebRequest reading the cached PNG. Extract and defang any URL/host in the command. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the interpreter process tree, and block the resolved delivery domain and C2 IPs (91.92.240.100, 213.139.77.109, 194.230.225.18) at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: search the same host for follow-on Inno Setup installer + python.exe from AppData and connections to blockchain RPC providers (EtherHiding) to confirm DeviceManager/CountLoader staging.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".png"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Cache\", @"Cache_Data", @"\Code Cache\", @"cache2\entries", @"\Chrome\User Data", @"\Edge\User Data", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles", @"\BraveSoftware\", @"\Opera Software\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has ".png"
| where CommandLine has_any ("\\Cache\\","Cache_Data","\\Code Cache\\","cache2\\entries","\\Chrome\\User Data","\\Edge\\User Data","\\Firefox\\Profiles","\\BraveSoftware\\","\\Opera Software\\")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DOUBLECUP delivery domain and /api/config endpoint contact AIDelivery High
Detects victim browsers reaching the DOUBLECUP landing/delivery domains (cloud-electronic.com, rigmadessignkit.com) and surfaces the structural DOUBLECUP config endpoint (URL ending in /api/config) that returns the steganographic image URL and browser-specific commands. Flags both the known IOC domains and the reusable endpoint signature. Rationale: cloud-electronic.com and rigmadessignkit.com are named campaign delivery domains; the article specifies the fixed endpoint https://{domain}/{slug}/api/config returning the DOUBLECUP config. Both are concrete, corroborated by SOCRadar/BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-doublecup-clickfix-service-hides-malware-in-browser-cache-images/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst or sandbox detonating the URL from a corporate host during research
  • Security proxy pre-fetch / URL-detonation appliance visiting the domain
  • Legitimate but unrelated site coincidentally exposing an /api/config path (only triggers combined with the IOC domains here)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which host/user reached the domain and whether the /api/config endpoint or a .png on the same host was subsequently fetched. 2) Contain: block the two domains and their resolved IPs org-wide; if the endpoint returned data, treat the host as staged and isolate it. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source host for the ClickFix script-from-cache activity (UC1) and any download of an Inno Setup installer, and sweep other hosts that resolved the same domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("cloud-electronic.com","rigmadessignkit.com")
| extend IsConfigEndpoint = RemoteUrl endswith "/api/config"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, IsConfigEndpoint, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("cloud-electronic.com","rigmadessignkit.com")
| extend IsConfigEndpoint = Url endswith "/api/config"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, IsConfigEndpoint
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DOUBLECUP / CountLoader / DeviceManager C2 IP connections AICommand & Control Medium
Alerting detection for outbound connections to the campaign's hardcoded infrastructure: the DOUBLECUP license-panel/open-directory host 213.139.77.109 (:9090), the DeviceManager/CountLoader C2 91.92.240.100 (EtherHiding-resolved, dns://91.92.240.100), and 194.230.225.18. Surfaces the initiating process for immediate triage. Rationale: 213.139.77.109:9090 (DOUBLECUP license panel open directory), 91.92.240.100 (DeviceManager/CountLoader C2, confirmed dns://91.92.240.100 by SOCRadar), and 194.230.225.18 are article-supplied IOCs corroborated by SOCRadar/BleepingComputer. Direct IP IOC match = alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-doublecup-clickfix-service-hides-malware-in-browser-cache-images/

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/blue-team validation connections to these IOCs from a research host
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse if the C2 IP is later reassigned to benign services (validate against current threat intel dates)
  • Security scanner sweeping the /24 for exposure
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName — a browser suggests delivery-stage, python.exe/unsigned binary suggests active RAT C2; note port 9090 for 213.139.77.109. 2) Contain: block all three IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and capture the initiating process binary for reversing. 3) Hunt: enumerate every internal host that touched any of the three IPs, and correlate with DNS/HTTP tunneling patterns to 91.92.240.100 indicative of DeviceManager beaconing.

DeviceManager RAT: embedded Python spawned from Inno Setup installer in user space AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the DeviceManager install routine where a Delphi-compiled Inno Setup installer extracts a full embedded Python environment and spawns python.exe/pythonw.exe from an AppData/Temp path. Filters to installers/droppers launched from user-writable directories to catch the RAT's staging before C2. Rationale: Article: DeviceManager is 'distributed as a Delphi-compiled Inno Setup installer... extracts a full embedded Python environment to spawn the Python malware'. python.exe running from AppData/Temp (esp. Inno Setup's \Temp\is-*.tmp\ extraction dirs) with a dropper parent is the concrete install signature. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-doublecup-clickfix-service-hides-malware-in-browser-cache-images/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate portable/embedded Python apps (some updaters, game mods, PyInstaller-onedir tools) running from AppData
  • Developer virtualenvs or conda envs placed under user profile directories
  • Data-science notebooks launching python from user-space installs
  • Inno Setup installers for benign software that bundle Python (e.g. some engineering tools)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("conda.exe","pip.exe","code.exe","pycharm64.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "site-packages\\pip"
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the python payload directory for an embedded interpreter + encrypted blob and check whether the parent is a recently-downloaded Inno Setup .exe; hash and reputation-check both. 2) Contain: if the process subsequently spawns cmd.exe/PowerShell or reaches blockchain RPC/91.92.240.100, isolate and kill the tree. 3) Hunt: look for the CIS-locale self-deletion pattern (UC6) and EtherHiding RPC lookups (UC5) on the same host to confirm DeviceManager.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\AppData\Local\Programs\", @"\Temp\is-")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\is-")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\python.exe","\\pythonw.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Roaming\\","\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\","\\Temp\\is-")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceManager EtherHiding: non-browser process resolving C2 via blockchain RPC AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts DeviceManager's EtherHiding dead-drop resolution, where the Python RAT queries public Ethereum/Polygon RPC providers to read a smart contract and derive its live C2 (dns://91.92.240.100). Scopes to non-browser initiators (python and AppData/Temp binaries) to strip out legitimate wallet/browser web3 traffic. Rationale: Article: DeviceManager 'utilizes EtherHiding to resolve its C2... dynamically resolves its active C2 nodes via Ethereum/Polygon smart contracts'; SOCRadar confirms it decrypts to dns://91.92.240.100. A Python/AppData process (not a browser) hitting public ETH/Polygon RPC providers is the EtherHiding tell. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://www.cynet.com/blog/clickfix-reloaded-from-mass-hijackloader-infections-to-stealth-etherhiding-rats/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate crypto/web3 desktop apps or trading bots written in Python querying Infura/Alchemy
  • Blockchain data-analytics or node-monitoring scripts run by developers
  • Wallet software using an embedded Python component (rare)
  • CI/CD or research jobs pulling on-chain data via public RPC
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "web3" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Program Files\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary is not a sanctioned web3/crypto app; inspect the python path (AppData/Temp = suspicious) and any subsequent DNS/HTTP to 91.92.240.100. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the resolved C2 and the smart-contract RPC endpoints for that process, and capture the python payload. 3) Hunt: decode any DNS-tunneling traffic to 91.92.240.100, and check for the Inno Setup+Python install (UC4) and CIS-locale self-deletion (UC6) to fully attribute DeviceManager.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceManager anti-analysis self-deletion: python spawns cmd rmdir + schtasks /delete AIInstallation Medium
Detects DeviceManager's CIS-locale self-destruct routine where the Python RAT, on detecting a Commonwealth of Independent States language, deletes its scheduled task and removes its installation directory via cmd.exe. Anchors on python.exe as parent spawning cmd deleting an AppData/Temp path or schtasks /delete. Rationale: Article: on CIS-language detection DeviceManager 'removes its scheduled task, deletes its installation directory via cmd.exe, and terminates process execution'. A python.exe parent spawning cmd rmdir of AppData/Temp or schtasks /delete is a tight, article-specific self-destruct signature. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/doublecup-uses-clickfix-and-cached-pngs.html
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1053.005 T1614.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python installers/uninstallers cleaning their own temp extraction dirs
  • Python-based build/test tooling removing scratch dirs and cleanup tasks
  • IT automation written in Python that manages scheduled tasks via schtasks
  • PyInstaller/py2exe onefile bootstrap cleaning its _MEI temp folder (uses cmd/del under Temp)
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "_MEI" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Program Files\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the deleted directory path and the schtasks task name from the command lines before artifacts vanish; check the host locale/keyboard layout for CIS settings that triggered self-destruct. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve memory — self-deletion means disk forensics may be gone; pull the parent python image if still present. 3) Hunt: correlate with prior EtherHiding RPC lookups (UC5), the Inno Setup+Python install (UC4), and C2 to 91.92.240.100 to reconstruct the full DeviceManager chain across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rmdir","rd /s","rd /q"," del ") and ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\"))
   or (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/delete")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("rmdir","rd /s","rd /q"," del ") and CommandLine has_any ("AppData","\\Temp\\"))
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "/delete")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DeviceManager CIS-Locale Self-Deletion via Python-Spawned cmd/schtasks

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)

let BadIPs     = dynamic(["213.139.77.109", "91.92.240.100", "194.230.225.18"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["cloud-electronic.com", "rigmadessignkit.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
