    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"

| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA Adds Exploited N-able N-central Flaw to KEV After Customer Compromises

The Hacker News
2026-08-04 11 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added a high-severity security flaw impacting N-able N-central to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog following reports of active exploitation in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-18577 (CVSS score: 8.2), is a case of incomplete patching for CVE-2026-18556 (CVSS score: 8.2) that allows

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Inbound/outbound connections to N-central intrusion VPN exit-node IOC IPs · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] N-central intrusion: svchost.exe masquerading in a user Documents folder · [LLM] Cloudflared tunnel service persistence on N-central-managed host · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS/network to N-central intrusion Synology QuickConnect tunnel domains · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
N-central intrusion: svchost.exe masquerading in a user Documents folder AIInstallation High
Hunts the N-able N-central (CVE-2026-18577) post-exploitation payload drop: a binary named 'svchost.exe' written into a user's Documents folder. Legitimate svchost.exe only ever lives under \Windows\System32 or \SysWOW64, so any svchost.exe under a Documents path is a masqueraded implant deployed via the abused Take Control feature. Rationale: Uses N-able/Huntress-published IOC verbatim: a file called 'svchost.exe' in the device users' Documents folder. Legit svchost.exe never resides in Documents, making the path+name pair high-fidelity. Corroborated by Huntress, BleepingComputer and Arctic Wolf write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/n-able-warns-of-n-central-auth-bypass-flaw-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2026-18556-cve-2026-18577/
ATT&CKT1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or admin extracting a legitimate Windows binary into a Documents\backup folder for analysis
  • Malware-analysis sandbox VMs storing sample copies of svchost.exe under a user profile
  • EDR/AV quarantine-restore actions dropping copies of svchost.exe into a user-writable path
  • Backup/restore software temporarily staging system files under a user Documents share
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe") and not (FolderPath has @"\Documents\Malware" or FolderPath has @"\Documents\Samples")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull SHA256 of the dropped svchost.exe and the InitiatingProcess that wrote it; check whether the host is an N-central-managed endpoint and whether a 'Cloudflared' service exists. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the endpoint, kill the masqueraded process, and quarantine the file; suspend the N-central Take Control agent's ability to push to this host. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all N-central-managed endpoints for the same file name/hash, for a Cloudflared service, and for connections to the four IOC VPN IPs; verify N-central is patched to 2026.3 HF1 / 2026.3.1.7.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Documents\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloudflared tunnel service persistence on N-central-managed host AIInstallation High
Detects registration of a Windows service named 'Cloudflared' — the persistence mechanism deployed after CVE-2026-18577 exploitation of N-able N-central. Attackers install cloudflared as a service to establish a covert outbound tunnel and blend malicious traffic into legitimate Cloudflare infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the N-able-published IOC 'a registered service name called Cloudflared'. Detecting the service-key write (7045/registry Services\Cloudflared) is a durable persistence pivot. Cross-checked against Huntress and Security Affairs coverage of the KEV listing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://securityaffairs.com/196585/security/u-s-cisa-adds-a-n-able-n-central-flaw-to-its-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog.html • https://www.rapid7.com/db/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-18577/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An org that legitimately deploys Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) as a service for zero-trust access to internal apps
  • IT automation/GPO rolling out cloudflared to a fleet during the same window
  • A developer testing Cloudflare Tunnel on their workstation
  • MSP tooling that legitimately bundles cloudflared for remote support
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "cloudflared.exe service install" or RegistryValueData has @"\Documents\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the service ImagePath — if it points to a Documents-folder svchost.exe or an unsigned binary, treat as malicious; confirm no change ticket authorized cloudflared. Step 2 (contain): Stop and delete the service, block the tunnel egress at the firewall, and isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate cloudflared config/tunnel tokens, pivot on the writing process's parent chain back to N-central Take Control, and sweep the fleet for the service plus the four IOC IPs.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\Cloudflared"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (7045, 4697)
| where ServiceName =~ "Cloudflared" or ServiceFileName has "cloudflared"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound/outbound connections to N-central intrusion VPN exit-node IOC IPs AIExploitation Medium
Flags any host communicating with the six IP addresses tied to the CVE-2026-18577 N-able N-central compromises (Mullvad/NordVPN exit nodes, one with prior brute-force history). Includes 173.249.252.200, the IP seen abusing the default 'MSP Support' Take Control session username. Rationale: Uses the four IP IOCs from the article plus two additional Huntress-attributed IPs. 173.249.252.200 is the source of the malicious 'MSP Support' Take Control session; 37.19.210.32 has prior brute-force history. Confirmed by Huntress and the HackerNews KEV article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/cisa-adds-exploited-n-able-n-central.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/08/03/cve-2026-18577-n-able-n-central-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133 T1078
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate remote worker or admin routing through Mullvad/NordVPN whose exit node happens to match an IOC IP
  • Threat-intel enrichment or sandbox detonation reaching out to the IOC IPs
  • Shared VPN exit-node IP reassigned to benign traffic after the campaign
  • Security scanner/pentest tooling configured to egress via a commercial VPN
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether the local endpoint is the N-central server or a managed endpoint, and whether the connection coincides with a Take Control session using the 'MSP Support' username. Step 2 (contain): Block the IOC IPs at perimeter and host firewall, terminate active N-central Take Control sessions, and rotate N-central admin credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Review N-central Take Control activity logs for the MSP Support username, look for svchost.exe drops and Cloudflared services on any host that touched these IPs, and confirm the KEV patch (2026.3 HF1) is applied.
let iocIPs = dynamic(["173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","68.235.46.214","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181"]);

| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS/network to N-central intrusion Synology QuickConnect tunnel domains AICommand & Control High
Detects resolution of or connections to the three attacker relay domains (Synology QuickConnect / synology.me) used as tunnel endpoints in the CVE-2026-18577 N-able N-central compromises. These act as covert command-and-control / data-relay infrastructure disguised as legitimate consumer NAS services. Rationale: Uses the three attacker-controlled Synology QuickConnect domains tied to the campaign. These are specific FQDNs (not a wildcard), so resolution by any managed endpoint is high-fidelity C2 signal. Cross-checked against Huntress and the HackerNews KEV coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/cisa-adds-exploited-n-able-n-central.html • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2026-18556-cve-2026-18577/
ATT&CKT1572 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Synology NAS owner in the org syncing to their personal QuickConnect address (unlikely to match these exact hostnames)
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation resolving the IOC domains during analysis
  • DNS logging appliance replaying/seeding IOC feeds that include these domains
  • Passive DNS mirror or security research tooling querying the domains for enrichment
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify which process on the host initiated the resolution (cloudflared.exe or masqueraded svchost.exe strongly confirm intrusion) and whether the host is N-central-managed. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block the three domains at DNS and egress, isolate the resolving host, and kill the tunnel process. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate resolving hosts with the Cloudflared service and svchost.exe IOCs, review N-central Take Control logs for the originating session, and block the associated VPN exit-node IPs.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| where DnsQuery in~ (iocDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)

Installation. keyv/cacheable npm compromise: node executing preinstall setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js dropper AIInstallation High
Hunts the Mini Shai-Hulud preinstall dropper shipped in the compromised keyv, cacheable, flat-cache, file-entry-cache and ecto npm releases (Aug 4 2026). Fires when node runs the malicious lifecycle script setup.mjs under an npm/pnpm/yarn install, or when any process references the unique second-stage filenames Math_Symbol.js / math_init.js. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact lifecycle-hook string ('preinstall':'node setup.mjs') plus the byte-identical second-stage filenames Math_Symbol.js and math_init.js, which are unique to this campaign and not benign npm artifacts. Cross-checked Aikido, Wiz and Snyk advisory SNYK-JS-KEYV-18515941. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/keyv-and-friends-compromised-in-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/large-scale-npm-pypi-supply-chain-campaign-suspected-across-multiple-popular-packages
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate unrelated package that genuinely ships a benign setup.mjs preinstall script (rare, but exists) run under npm
  • Internal monorepo tooling that names a build script setup.mjs and invokes it via node during install
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a sandbox for analysis
  • A developer manually running 'node setup.mjs' for a non-malicious project of their own
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs" and not (FolderPath has "node_modules") and not ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the hitting host, pull the full node process tree and confirm the working directory is inside node_modules for keyv/cacheable/flat-cache/file-entry-cache/ecto; hash the on-disk setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js and compare to the campaign SHA256s. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/CI runner from network, kill the node and any bun child process, and treat all developer/CI-scoped tokens as exposed — DO NOT revoke GitHub tokens yet if gh-token-monitor is present. 3) HUNT: Search the org's lockfiles and private mirrors for the affected versions, look for bun download from GitHub, .claude/.vscode hook files, and gh-token-monitor persistence before rotating credentials from a clean system.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js")
   or (FileName in~ ("node.exe","node") and ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
       and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","npx","pnpm","yarn","preinstall"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js")
   or (TargetProcessName has "node" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
       and ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","npx","pnpm","yarn"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

keyv npm compromise: malicious payload file drop by SHA256 (setup.mjs / Math_Symbol.js) AIDelivery Medium
Highest-fidelity detection for the keyv/cacheable compromise: matches the two byte-identical payload files by their published SHA256 across every affected release, or the unique second-stage filenames written into node_modules. Snyk confirmed all nine retrievable tarballs carried the identical 29,918-byte setup.mjs and 727,680-byte Math_Symbol.js. Rationale: Uses the article's exact published SHA256 values for the 29,918-byte setup.mjs and 727,680-byte Math_Symbol.js — Snyk verified these are identical across all affected releases, so a hash match is a confirmed compromise regardless of which package name delivered it. Corroborated by Aikido and Wiz. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/keyv-and-friends-compromised-in-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel or EDR feed writing the sample to disk during automated IOC ingestion
  • A malware analyst intentionally staging the file in a lab
  • A backup/restore job re-materializing a quarantined copy of the payload
  • An unrelated legitimate file coincidentally named math_init.js under node_modules (mitigated by requiring the hash for the strongest signal)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the SHA256 match is a true hit (hash match = confirmed campaign payload); identify which package/version under node_modules delivered it and whether this is a dev workstation or CI runner. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, quarantine the file, and inventory which credentials that identity could reach (GitHub/npm tokens, cloud creds, kubeconfig, Vault). Disable gh-token-monitor persistence BEFORE revoking any GitHub token. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the delivering package name across all repos/lockfiles/mirrors, pin to last-known-good (e.g. flat-cache 6.1.23, cacheable-request 13.0.19, cache-manager 7.2.9), and rotate all exposed secrets from a clean host.

keyv npm compromise: IDE-hook persistence files planted in .claude / .vscode AIInstallation High
Detects the second execution path from GitHub commit d8c850c7 — malicious setup.mjs / math_init.js written into a repo's .claude or .vscode directory so a Claude SessionStart command or a VS Code folderOpen task auto-runs the payload when a developer or coding agent opens the checkout. A .mjs/init script inside these config dirs is abnormal. Rationale: Anchors on the exact artifact set from GitHub commit d8c850c7 (.claude/setup.mjs, .claude/math_init.js, .vscode/setup.mjs) — an executable .mjs/init script inside IDE/agent config directories is not a normal project layout and represents the workspace-trust execution path the article highlights. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/keyv-and-friends-compromised-in-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately stores a helper setup.mjs inside .vscode for local task automation (uncommon but possible)
  • A developer copying a template repo that includes .vscode task scripts
  • IDE extension scaffolding that writes .mjs helpers into .vscode
  • Git clone/checkout materializing these files from a trusted internal repo (verify provenance before dismissing)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the flagged .claude/.vscode file and check for obfuscated loader content or references to Math_Symbol.js/math_init.js/Bun; identify the repo and whether it was opened in an IDE or coding agent (VS Code folderOpen / Claude SessionStart). 2) CONTAIN: Remove the hook files, revoke workspace trust for the repo, and isolate the host if the task/SessionStart already fired (correlate with node/bun process events). 3) HUNT: Grep all internal repos for .claude/.vscode setup.mjs, review recent commits by the compromised maintainer identity, and check for gh-token-monitor persistence and Bun downloads on the same host.

keyv npm compromise: Bun runtime executing second-stage math_init.js / Math_Symbol.js AICommand & Control High
Detects the loader's second execution stage — when Bun is absent the loader fetches Bun 1.3.13 from GitHub and uses it to run the 727,680-byte second stage (Math_Symbol.js / math_init.js). A bun process executing these filenames, especially spawned by a node setup.mjs parent, is high-signal for this campaign. Rationale: Uses the article's specifics: the loader fetches Bun 1.3.13 and runs the second stage named math_init.js / Math_Symbol.js. Bun executing those exact filenames, or Bun spawned by a setup.mjs parent, is not a normal developer pattern. Corroborated by Upwind's execution-flow write-up ('bun run index.js' second stage). Cross-checked against: • https://www.upwind.io/feed/large-scale-npm-pypi-supply-chain-campaign-suspected-across-multiple-popular-packages • https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1587.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Bun-native project that legitimately has a source file named math_init.js (mitigated by requiring the setup.mjs parent or exact campaign filenames)
  • A developer who genuinely uses Bun and just installed it from GitHub
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample
  • CI pipeline that legitimately runs bun against a project script (verify parent is not setup.mjs)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the bun parent chain traces to node setup.mjs / an npm install of an affected package; check for a freshly downloaded bun binary in temp and outbound connections to github.com for the Bun 1.3.13 release. 2) CONTAIN: Kill the bun process, isolate the host, and treat GitHub/npm tokens, cloud creds, private keys, DB strings, Vault and Kubernetes SA tokens as harvested — disable gh-token-monitor before revoking GitHub tokens. 3) HUNT: Look across the fleet for bun-spawned-by-setup.mjs, the campaign payload hashes, and IDE-hook files; rotate all reachable secrets from a clean system.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "bun"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js","math_init.js")
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

keyv npm compromise: gh-token-monitor credential-persistence artifacts (macOS/Linux) AIInstallation High
Detects the gh-token-monitor persistence dropped by the Mini Shai-Hulud second stage — a monitor that watches a stolen GitHub token and runs a supplied handler when the token stops working. Fires on creation of gh-token-monitor.sh, the ~/.config/gh-token-monitor directory, or a process referencing gh-token-monitor. CRITICAL: this persistence must be disabled before any GitHub token revocation. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named persistence mechanism (gh-token-monitor) and the artifact names corroborated by Wiz/Upwind (~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh, ~/.config/gh-token-monitor/). The name is unique to this malware family and carries the critical operational caveat to disable it before token revocation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.upwind.io/feed/large-scale-npm-pypi-supply-chain-campaign-suspected-across-multiple-popular-packages • https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1546.004 T1543 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A homegrown ops script legitimately named gh-token-monitor (extremely unlikely given the exact name)
  • A researcher recreating the persistence artifact in a lab
  • A backup restoring a previously infected home directory
  • Endpoint IOC-sweep tooling writing the filename into a report path under a scan directory
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Locate gh-token-monitor.sh and ~/.config/gh-token-monitor plus any LaunchAgent/systemd unit referencing it; confirm which GitHub token it is watching. 2) CONTAIN: Disable and remove the monitor and its LaunchAgent/systemd service FIRST, then isolate the host — revoking the GitHub token before disabling the monitor can trigger the malware's handler. 3) HUNT: After the monitor is neutralized, rotate the exposed GitHub/npm tokens, cloud creds, private keys and Vault/K8s tokens from a clean system, and sweep the fleet for the payload hashes, bun second-stage execution, and IDE-hook files.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "gh-token-monitor.sh"
   or FolderPath has "gh-token-monitor"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "gh-token-monitor.sh" or TargetFilePath has "gh-token-monitor"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, DvcAction, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["d584f9b6af48b7ed1f93713944f033783bf149e1c25e1643eb8c0e9df5dc7782", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CornFlake persistence: 'Cloud Sync Service' autostart pointing to %AppData% · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CornFlake/ChocoShell C2 egress to CaptiveCrunch IPs or known malware hash · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Storm-2945 Entra ID sign-in / device-code auth from CaptiveCrunch infrastructure · [LLM] ChocoShell Wi-Fi credential theft via netsh wlan key=clear under PowerShell · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CaptiveCrunch DNS hijack: endpoint using Storm-2945 attacker DNS resolver AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoints whose configured DNS resolver, or DNS/HTTP egress on port 53, points to the six Storm-2945 (Midnight Blizzard) CaptiveCrunch relay IPs. This is the network-layer AiTM primitive that redirects hotel Wi-Fi victims to fake M365 portals and ClickFix update pages. Rationale: Anchored on the six confirmed CaptiveCrunch relay IPs cross-checked against the Microsoft Security Blog and ReliaQuest threat spotlight; a corporate endpoint configured to resolve DNS against these IPs is effectively AiTM'd. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1040
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A traveling laptop legitimately picked up a hotel captive-portal DNS that happens to share an ASN block (verify exact IP match, not CIDR)
  • Security research/sandbox host deliberately resolving against these IOCs
  • Threat-intel or honeypot appliance beaconing to the IPs for tracking
  • Corporate proxy egress where the recursive resolver IP was recently re-numbered
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(DnsAddresses) and ConnectedNetworks !has "CorporateManaged"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DeviceNetworkInfo DnsAddresses exact-match one of the six IPs and identify the network (hotel/conference SSID via ConnectedNetworks); check whether the device is a road-warrior laptop off-VPN. 2) Contain: force the device onto managed VPN/cellular, flush and re-pin trusted DNS, and quarantine if any subsequent M365 sign-in or ClickFix process is seen. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for connections to the ms365-* phishing domains, ClickFix process spawns, and any Entra sign-in from these IPs in the next 24h.
DeviceNetworkInfo

| where DnsAddresses has_any ("31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, NetworkAdapterName, DnsAddresses, DefaultGateways, ConnectedNetworks, IPAddresses
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ServerIPAddress in ("31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ServerIPAddress, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch M365 phishing portal domain resolution (ms365-*/owa-ms365) AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS resolution or web connections to the four Storm-2945 Microsoft 365 look-alike login domains used after captive-portal DNS hijack to harvest credentials and Entra tokens. Exact-domain match, so near-zero benign overlap. Rationale: The four M365 look-alike domains are named directly in the article's pre-extracted IOCs and match the Microsoft/ReliaQuest 'phishing pages that impersonate Microsoft 365 login portals' claim; exact FQDN match makes this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://cyberinsider.com/microsoft-links-hotel-wi-fi-hacks-to-russian-midnight-blizzard-hackers/

Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platform intentionally hosting look-alike domains for training
  • Analyst detonating the IOC in a sandbox that ships telemetry to prod
  • Threat-intel crawler / URL-scanner enriching these domains
  • Typo-squat parking page unrelated to the campaign resolving the same string (verify against IP IOCs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify user + device that resolved the domain and whether a browser process followed the lookup; check if the user was on hotel/conference Wi-Fi. 2) Contain: revoke the user's M365 refresh tokens and force MFA re-registration/password reset, block the four domains at the proxy/DNS sinkhole. 3) Hunt: review SigninLogs for successful auth from CaptiveCrunch IPs, and check the device for CornFlake persistence and %AppData% drops.

Storm-2945 Entra ID sign-in / device-code auth from CaptiveCrunch infrastructure AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects successful Microsoft Entra ID sign-ins originating from the six CaptiveCrunch relay IPs — the endpoint of the device-code and portal phishing flows that steal M365 session tokens. Because the source IPs are confirmed attacker infrastructure, any successful auth from them is high-fidelity account takeover. Rationale: Uses the six confirmed CaptiveCrunch IPs as the sign-in source anchor for the device-code/portal token-theft flow described by Microsoft; a successful Entra auth from known SVR relay infrastructure is inherently alerting-grade. Falcon left empty because Entra sign-in telemetry is not reliably shipped to FDR. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html

  • Security team replaying stolen-token IOCs in a test tenant
  • Threat-intel platform performing authenticated API validation from a research host
  • A managed identity/service principal misattributed to the IP
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName != "Test-Token-Validation"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the UPN, app, and whether the auth used device code or a stolen session token (check AuthenticationRequirement/ClientAppUsed and whether MFA was satisfied without user prompt). 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens for the user, disable the session, reset credentials, and disable Entra device-code flow if not required per Microsoft's guidance. 3) Hunt: enumerate mailbox rule creation, OAuth app consents, and downstream access from the same IPs; check the user's endpoint for CornFlake/ChocoShell.

CaptiveCrunch ClickFix: explorer.exe Run-dialog spawning download cradle AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the ClickFix delivery pattern where a fake browser/OS update page tricks the user into pasting a command into the Windows Run dialog, causing explorer.exe to spawn powershell/cmd/mshta/curl with an inline download of CornFlake. Targets the Run-dialog parent chain, distinct from Office- or browser-child execution. Rationale: Targets the article's 'ClickFix prompts for user verification' fake-update chain via the distinctive explorer.exe (Run-dialog) parent spawning a download cradle — a different process-tree pivot than the excluded browser/Office child-execution rules. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user running a legitimate one-liner from Win+R to fetch a script from an internal repo
  • IT deployment tooling that uses curl/Invoke-WebRequest launched via desktop shortcut (explorer parent)
  • Developer testing an HTA or web-download command interactively
  • Browser 'open with' handoffs that transit explorer.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\\\corp\\", "intranet", "sccm", "internal.") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the command line and resolve the download URL/IP; confirm whether the user was on public Wi-Fi and had just viewed an update prompt. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the resolved URL/IP, and capture the dropped payload from %AppData% for hashing against the CornFlake IOCs. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a %AppData% executable copy, 'Cloud Sync Service' persistence, and egress to the six CaptiveCrunch IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mshta","curl","Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","DownloadString","DownloadFile",".hta","http://","https://")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "explorer.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("mshta","curl","Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","DownloadString","DownloadFile",".hta","http://","https://")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake persistence: 'Cloud Sync Service' autostart pointing to %AppData% AIInstallation High
Detects CornFlake's persistence installs — Windows service registrations, registry Run keys and named tasks masquerading as 'Cloud Sync Service' with an image path in %AppData%. Also catches the watchdog re-registration where autostart values are rewritten to an AppData binary. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit persistence detail — CornFlake disguising as 'Cloud Sync Service', copying to %AppData%, and using service/Run-key/task registrations plus a watchdog — to anchor a high-fidelity autostart-in-AppData signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://cybernews.com/news/russian-hackers-hotel-wifi-malware-midnight-blizzard/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1547.001 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate cloud-sync agents (OneDrive/Dropbox/Box) that install per-user autostart from AppData — verify the exact 'Cloud Sync Service' string, not any sync tool
  • Electron/Squirrel apps that self-update and register Run keys in AppData
  • IT-packaged user-scope software deployed via Intune to AppData
  • Browser auto-update helpers writing Run values
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryValueData has_any ("OneDrive","Dropbox","Box.exe","GoogleDriveFS") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the exact value name/data and the InitiatingProcess — a Run/service value literally named 'Cloud Sync Service' pointing at a random-named %AppData% exe is malicious; hash the target binary against the CornFlake SHA256 IOCs. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove all four persistence types (service, Run key, task, plus the watchdog process) simultaneously to defeat re-registration, and delete the AppData payload. 3) Hunt: check for ChocoShell PowerShell credential theft, C2 to the six IPs, and identical persistence on peer hosts.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where (RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" or RegistryKey has @"\Services\")
| where RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\" or RegistryValueData has "Cloud Sync Service" or RegistryValueName =~ "Cloud Sync Service"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" or RegistryKey has @"\Services\")
| where RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\" or RegistryValueData has "Cloud Sync Service" or RegistryValue has "Cloud Sync Service"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake/ChocoShell C2 egress to CaptiveCrunch IPs or known malware hash AICommand & Control Medium
Detects endpoint egress to the six Storm-2945 C2/relay IPs, or any network activity initiated by a process whose SHA256 matches the two named CornFlake/ChocoShell samples. Combines network IOCs with hash IOCs on a single table for high-confidence C2 identification. Rationale: Fuses the six confirmed C2/relay IPs with the two named CornFlake/ChocoShell SHA256 samples (both cross-checked against the Microsoft blog and secondary reporting); DeviceNetworkEvents carries InitiatingProcessSHA256 so both IOC classes match on one table. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst sandbox detonation of the CornFlake sample beaconing to the C2
  • Threat-intel scanner probing the IPs for liveness
  • Hosting-provider IP reassignment putting a benign service on a former C2 address (verify recency)
  • Corporate honeypot deliberately interacting with the IOCs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and whether its hash matches the CornFlake/ChocoShell IOCs; determine data volume sent (possible exfil). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the six IPs at the perimeter, and revoke the associated user's M365 tokens (CornFlake steals session tokens). 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the two SHA256 hashes, 'Cloud Sync Service' persistence, and any peer hosts contacting the same IPs.

ChocoShell Wi-Fi credential theft via netsh wlan key=clear under PowerShell AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts ChocoShell's in-memory harvesting of Wi-Fi credentials — netsh wlan show profile with key=clear (which prints plaintext PSKs) launched by a script interpreter. This Wi-Fi-password extraction is a distinctive ChocoShell behavior alongside its browser cookie/token theft. Rationale: The article explicitly lists Wi-Fi credential theft as a ChocoShell capability; netsh wlan show profile key=clear is the canonical way to dump plaintext PSKs, and pairing it with a script-interpreter parent separates the malware from routine admin use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://cybernews.com/news/russian-hackers-hotel-wifi-malware-midnight-blizzard/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Help-desk / field IT dumping saved Wi-Fi keys during a connectivity troubleshoot
  • Endpoint onboarding scripts that inventory saved wireless profiles
  • A user running a known 'export my Wi-Fi passwords' utility
  • MDM/RMM automation collecting wireless profile data
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("MDMDiagnostics","support","helpdesk_wifi_inventory") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the full parent chain — if the powershell/cmd parent itself descends from explorer (ClickFix) or an AppData binary, treat as ChocoShell; check for concurrent browser Login Data / cookie access. 2) Contain: isolate the host, rotate the exposed Wi-Fi PSKs and the user's M365 credentials/tokens. 3) Hunt: look for browser credential-store reads, C2 to the six IPs, and CornFlake 'Cloud Sync Service' persistence on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "netsh.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "wlan" and ProcessCommandLine has "profile" and ProcessCommandLine has "key" and ProcessCommandLine has "clear"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "netsh.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "wlan" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "profile" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "key" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "clear"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Wi-Fi cleartext key extraction via netsh under script interpreter
id: b6c3f2a8-70e5-4d19-9c48-3a2e7b1d05c6
description: netsh wlan show profile key=clear launched by powershell/cmd, consistent with ChocoShell Wi-Fi credential theft
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1539
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\netsh.exe'

      - 'wlan'
      - 'profile'
      - 'key'
      - 'clear'
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\netsh.exe OR *\\NETSH.EXE) @CommandLine:(*wlan* AND *profile* AND *key* AND *clear*) @ParentImage:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\cmd.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\netsh\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)wlan", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)profile", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)key\\s*=\\s*clear", field=CommandLine)
| ParentBaseFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="netsh.exe" Processes.process="*wlan*" Processes.process="*profile*" Processes.process="*key*clear*" Processes.parent_process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

     | rename dest AS src]
