Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c") or SHA1 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c") or MD5 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c") or SHA1 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c") or MD5 in~ ("918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593", "be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-18556", "CVE-2026-18577")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-18556", "CVE-2026-18577")

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Silver Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process deletes/tampers Chrome passkey_enclave_state to force re-onboarding
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Golden Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process reads chrome.exe memory to scrape the security domain secret · [LLM] Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process accessing Google passkey credential store (LevelDB + enclave state)
Silver Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process deletes/tampers Chrome passkey_enclave_state to force re-onboarding AIInstallation High
Hunts an unprivileged process (other than chrome.exe / Google updater) deleting, renaming, or modifying Chrome's local passkey state file `passkey_enclave_state`, the exact precondition Unit 42's Silver Pass-ta-key uses to force Chrome to re-register so the attacker can enroll their own user-verification key. Article-specific because it keys on the named FIDO enclave state file under the Chrome User Data profile, not generic file deletion. Rationale: Keys on the exact named local FIDO state file `passkey_enclave_state` under `\Google\Chrome\User Data\` that Unit 42 says must be deleted/invalidated to trigger Silver Pass-ta-key re-onboarding; only Chrome itself and the Google updater legitimately touch this file, so a non-Chrome writer is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/google-synced-passkey-malware-attack/
ATT&CKT1556 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chrome profile reset / corruption repair performed by the user deleting the profile folder via explorer.exe
  • Endpoint backup or migration tooling (e.g. profile-sync utilities) copying/removing the User Data directory
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine action removing files inside the Chrome profile
  • Disk-cleanup or CCleaner-style tools purging browser profile artifacts
  • IT reimaging scripts wiping %LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","ccleaner.exe","backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcess (path, SHA256, signer) that deleted/modified passkey_enclave_state; confirm it is not chrome.exe/Google updater and check whether the user was actively resetting Chrome. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block/hash-ban the offending binary, and force the user to re-enroll passkeys from a clean device and review recent logins to passkey-protected accounts (eBay, Google, etc.). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a follow-on process reading chrome.exe memory (Golden) or opening Sync Data\LevelDB, and check Google account for a newly registered device/verification key.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state"
| where ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","GoogleUpdateComRegisterShell64.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, ActionType, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state"
| where EventType in ("FileDeleted","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\"
| where ActingProcessName !has "chrome.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "GoogleUpdate" and ActingProcessName !has "updater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Chrome Process Tampering With Google Passkey Enclave State File
id: 6f3c2b9a-8d41-4e2f-9b77-1a5c0e7d4c11
description: Detects deletion/modification/rename of Chrome's passkey_enclave_state FIDO enclave file by a process other than Chrome or the Google updater, the precondition for Unit 42's Silver Pass-ta-key re-onboarding attack.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-pass-ta-key-attacks-let-malware-hijack-google-synced-passkeys/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1556
  - attack.t1070.004
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\passkey_enclave_state'
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
  filter_main:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\GoogleUpdate.exe'
      - '\updater.exe'
      - '\elevation_service.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_main
level: high
source:windows.sysmon (@EventID:23 OR @EventID:26) @TargetFilename:(*\\passkey_enclave_state OR *\\Passkey_enclave_state) @TargetFilename:(*\\Google\\Chrome\\User\ Data\\* OR *\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*) -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\GoogleUpdate.exe OR *\\updater.exe OR *\\elevation_service.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileDeleted TargetFileName=/passkey_enclave_state$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|GoogleUpdate|updater|elevation_service)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="passkey_enclave_state" (Filesystem.action=deleted OR Filesystem.action=modified OR Filesystem.action=renamed) AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*" NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="passkey_enclave_state" (Filesystem.action=deleted OR Filesystem.action=modified OR Filesystem.action=renamed) AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*" NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
Golden Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process reads chrome.exe memory to scrape the security domain secret AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a foreign process opening or reading the memory of chrome.exe, the technique Unit 42's Golden Pass-ta-key uses to extract the security-domain-secret (SDS) master key that decrypts all synced passkeys after forcing a re-registration. Article-specific because it targets browser-process memory access to chrome.exe (not LSASS) — the only place the SDS transiently lives after Google removed it from the FIDO log. Rationale: Unit 42 states the SDS master key 'remains accessible in Chrome's process memory' and can be extracted 'directly from memory' after a forced re-registration; a non-browser process opening chrome.exe with read/VM-read access (GrantedAccess masks) is the observable for that scrape. Marked hunting due to legitimate memory access by AV/crash handlers. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint AV/EDR (MsMpEng.exe, MsSense.exe) scanning or monitoring browser memory
  • Chrome's own crashpad_handler.exe collecting a crash minidump of chrome.exe
  • Browser management / DLP agents that inspect browser memory
  • Performance/telemetry tools (e.g. Sysinternals procdump run by an admin) dumping chrome.exe
  • Enterprise password-manager browser integrations reading browser state
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("procdump.exe","procdump64.exe","taskmgr.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("administrator")) and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceImage/InitiatingProcess (path, signer, SHA256, integrity level) and confirm it is not a known AV/crash/DLP agent; note the GrantedAccess mask (read/VM_READ is suspicious). 2) Contain: isolate host, capture a memory image before reboot, hash-ban the process, and treat all Google-synced passkeys as compromised — the SDS cannot be rotated, so force passkey re-creation on affected accounts. 3) Hunt: correlate with a preceding passkey_enclave_state deletion (Silver) on the same host and outbound transfer of Sync Data\LevelDB; review Google account device list for rogue enrollments.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("OpenProcessApiCall","ReadProcessMemoryApiCall")
| where FileName =~ "chrome.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","crashpad_handler.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, TargetProcess=FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("OpenProcessApiCall","ReadProcessMemoryApiCall")
| where FileName =~ "chrome.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","crashpad_handler.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, ActionType, TargetProcess=FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Foreign Process Reading Chrome Browser Process Memory (Golden Pass-ta-key SDS Scrape)
id: b2d9f4a1-3c67-4a08-9e21-77c4e0a9f3d2
description: Detects a non-browser, non-security process opening chrome.exe with memory-read access rights, consistent with Unit 42's Golden Pass-ta-key extraction of the security domain secret from Chrome process memory.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-pass-ta-key-attacks-let-malware-hijack-google-synced-passkeys/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1003
logsource:
  category: process_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetImage|endswith: '\chrome.exe'
    GrantedAccess:
      - '0x1010'
      - '0x1410'
      - '0x1438'
      - '0x143a'
      - '0x1F1FFF'
      - '0x1F3FFF'
      - '0x1FFFFF'
  filter_main:
    SourceImage|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\MsMpEng.exe'
      - '\MsSense.exe'
      - '\crashpad_handler.exe'
      - '\GoogleUpdate.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_main
level: medium
ENDPOINT
`sysmon` EventCode=10 TargetImage="*\\chrome.exe" NOT (SourceImage IN ("*\\chrome.exe","*\\msedge.exe","*\\MsMpEng.exe","*\\MsSense.exe","*\\SenseIR.exe","*\\crashpad_handler.exe","*\\GoogleUpdate.exe")) GrantedAccess IN ("0x1010","0x1410","0x1438","0x143a","0x1fffff","0x1f1fff","0x1f3fff") | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(GrantedAccess) as GrantedAccess by dest, user, SourceImage, TargetImage | sort - lastTime
Pass-ta-key: non-Chrome process accessing Google passkey credential store (LevelDB + enclave state) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a process other than Chrome opening, copying, or modifying the Google Password Manager passkey stores — `Sync Data\LevelDB` (WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records) and `passkey_enclave_state` (the TPM-wrapped device identity key) — under the Chrome User Data profile. Article-specific because these are the exact files Unit 42 abuses: the enclave key to sign forged assertions (Pass-ta-key) and the LevelDB records to recover private keys (Golden). Rationale: Targets the two exact stores Unit 42 names — `Sync Data\LevelDB` holding WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records and `passkey_enclave_state` holding the wrapped identity private key — under `\Google\Chrome\User Data\`; any non-Chrome process opening/copying these is the read side of Pass-ta-key signing and Golden decryption. Falcon FileOpenInfo is the strongest telemetry as it captures reads Defender/Sysmon do not. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/google-synced-passkey-malware-attack/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1606
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup/DLP agents enumerating the Chrome profile directory
  • Antivirus/EDR on-access scanning of the LevelDB files
  • Browser profile migration or enterprise browser-management tooling
  • Indexing/search services (e.g. Windows Search) touching profile files
  • Chrome update/repair helper processes not covered by the allowlist
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","backup.exe","OneDrive.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the accessing process (signer, SHA256, parent, cmdline) and whether it read `passkey_enclave_state` (assertion forging) vs `Sync Data\LevelDB` (record theft); confirm it is not backup/AV. 2) Contain: isolate host, hash-ban the binary, and treat synced passkeys as compromised — force re-enrollment and audit the Google account device/key list. 3) Hunt: pivot to whether the same process also read chrome.exe memory (Golden SDS scrape) or deleted the enclave state (Silver), and look for exfil of the copied LevelDB off-host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state") or (FolderPath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\"
| where ActionType in ("FileAccessed","FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","GoogleUpdateComRegisterShell64.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "passkey_enclave_state") or (TargetFilePath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\"
| where EventType in ("FileAccessed","FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName !has "chrome.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "GoogleUpdate" and ActingProcessName !has "updater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Chrome Process Accessing Google Passkey Credential Store
id: c41a7e58-9b2d-4d6a-8f0e-2b9d6c3a71ef
description: Detects a process other than Chrome/Google updater accessing the Google Password Manager passkey stores (Sync Data\LevelDB or passkey_enclave_state) under the Chrome User Data profile, per Unit 42 Pass-ta-key / Golden Pass-ta-key credential recovery.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-pass-ta-key-attacks-let-malware-hijack-google-synced-passkeys/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1606
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_store:
    - TargetFilename|endswith: '\passkey_enclave_state'

  selection_path:

level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\passkey_enclave_state OR *\\Sync\ Data\\LevelDB\\* OR *\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\*)) @TargetFilename:(*\\Google\\Chrome\\User\ Data\\* OR *\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*) -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\GoogleUpdate.exe OR *\\updater.exe)
#event_simpleName=/^(FileOpenInfo|FileWritten)$/ TargetFileName=/\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\/i
| TargetFileName=/(passkey_enclave_state$|\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\)/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|GoogleUpdate|updater|elevation_service)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="passkey_enclave_state" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\*") AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*" NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="passkey_enclave_state" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\*") AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*" NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Sequelize Oracle SQLi: TO_DATE/TO_TIMESTAMP quote-bypass payload in HTTP request AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP query strings / bodies carrying the CVE-2026-69240 payload shape — a parameter value beginning with TO_DATE( or TO_TIMESTAMP( followed by a quote break-out (||'', OR 1=1, --, UNION). This is the delivery vector that reaches Sequelize's vulnerable escape() path in the Oracle dialect. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC signature from the GHSA (`TO_DATE('0','Y')||'' OR 1=1--`): a param value opening with TO_DATE(/TO_TIMESTAMP( plus a break-out token. Legitimate query params never combine an Oracle date-cast function with `||''`/`OR 1=1`/`--`, making this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/sequelize/CVE-2026-69240/ • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-SEQUELIZE-2959225 • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-69240
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DAST/pentest tooling (sqlmap, Burp Scanner, Acunetix) firing SQLi payloads during authorized testing
  • An internal application that legitimately accepts Oracle TO_DATE(...) expressions as a search parameter (rare)
  • Security awareness / red-team exercises replaying known CVE payloads
  • WAF that decodes and logs the raw attack even though it blocked the request (still a true attempt, triage as such)
  • Copy/paste of Oracle SQL snippets into a free-text search field by a developer
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("<known-scanner-ip-placeholder>") // replace/remove if no sanctioned scanners; prefer excluding by scanner UserAgent when available
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (SrcIP, UriPath, Query) and confirm the target app uses Sequelize with dialect=oracle and version < 6.37.4; check the HTTP status/response size to judge whether injection succeeded. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, add a virtual-patch rule dropping TO_DATE(/TO_TIMESTAMP( in user input, and prioritise upgrading Sequelize to >= 6.37.4. 3) Hunt: pivot on SrcIP for other endpoints/params hit, and cross-check the Oracle audit UC (below) for the same window to confirm the payload actually executed at the DB.
union

New DOUBLECUP ClickFix service hides malware in browser cache images

BleepingComputer
2026-08-03 15 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new Russian loader-as-a-service named DOUBLECUP uses ClickFix attacks to hide malicious code in PNG images cached by victims' browsers, ultimately delivering CountLoader to Windows and macOS devices and a new remote access trojan named DeviceManager to Windows systems. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] DOUBLECUP ClickFix infrastructure: DNS/network to spoofed SaaS login IOC domains & IPs · [LLM] ClickFix clipboard-to-Run execution: RunMRU write + shell spawned from explorer · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Steganographic payload extraction from browser cache via certutil/findstr · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Public-IPv4 discovery by non-browser process (environmental keying for payload decryption) · [LLM] CountLoader macOS LaunchAgent recon: sw_vers/system_profiler/ioreg clustered under one parent · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DeviceManager EtherHiding: non-browser host querying Ethereum/Polygon RPC endpoints for C2 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DeviceManager DNS A/TXT tunneling for command retrieval and data exfiltration · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
DOUBLECUP ClickFix infrastructure: DNS/network to spoofed SaaS login IOC domains & IPs AIDelivery Medium
Hunts host resolution or connection to DOUBLECUP's known ClickFix delivery infrastructure — the fake NetSuite/Odoo/HubSpot login domains and the service's licensing/host IPs. Article-specific because it uses the exact IOCs SOCRadar tied to this campaign, not a generic phishing-domain heuristic. Rationale: Uses the exact SOCRadar-published IOC domains/IPs (login-netsuite.com, 213.139.77.109, 66.29.148.143). Cross-checked against the SOCRadar and The Hacker News write-ups of the same campaign — both list these SaaS-impersonation lures. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/doublecup-uses-clickfix-and-cached-pngs.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team detonating the sample in a sandbox that egresses to real infra
  • Threat-intel platform auto-enrichment resolving the IOC domains
  • A legitimately-registered lookalike domain later reclaimed by the impersonated vendor
  • URL-scanning proxy pre-fetching the domain on a user's behalf
  • Analyst manually browsing to the phishing page during triage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","smartscreen.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/user and the initiating process for the connection; confirm it was a user browser vs. a scanner/sandbox. 2) Contain: block the IOC domains/IPs at proxy/DNS/firewall and isolate the host if a non-browser process made the connection (indicates post-exec). 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to certutil/findstr browser-cache PNG extraction (UC2), RunMRU ClickFix artifacts (UC3), and outbound public-IP-check / blockchain-RPC calls (UC4/UC5).

Steganographic payload extraction from browser cache via certutil/findstr AIExploitation High
Hunts the DOUBLECUP first-stage recovery step where a pasted command uses findstr or certutil to locate a PNG in the browser cache (by exact file size) and decode the hidden payload. Article-specific: the extraction tool + browser-cache path + PNG combination is the campaign's signature. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's quote: findstr/certutil 'searches the browser cache for the PNG based on its exact file size' to recover the hidden payload. certutil/findstr touching a browser cache PNG is near-zero in benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/doublecup-uses-clickfix-and-cached-pngs.html
ATT&CKT1027.003 T1140 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/QA scripts grepping browser cache during app testing
  • Forensic/IR tooling extracting cached images during investigation
  • Backup software indexing AppData that shells out to findstr
  • Certificate tooling legitimately using certutil in a path that happens to contain 'Cache'
  • Browser-cache cleanup utilities enumerating .png files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","devenv.exe","msbuild.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and the parent process — a ClickFix chain shows explorer.exe/cmd.exe as parent and a specific byte-size filter. Recover the referenced PNG from cache for analysis. 2) Contain: isolate the host; kill the certutil/findstr and any child fileless second stage; capture memory. 3) Hunt: look for the follow-on public-IP lookup (UC4), blockchain-RPC C2 (UC5), CountLoader scheduled-task persistence, and DNS TXT tunneling (UC6) on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("certutil.exe","findstr.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Cache", "Cache_Data", "cache2", ".png")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Google\\Chrome", "Microsoft\\Edge", "Mozilla\\Firefox", "BraveSoftware", "Opera", "Cache")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("certutil.exe","findstr.exe")

| where CommandLine has_any ("Chrome","Edge","Mozilla","BraveSoftware","Opera","Cache")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ClickFix clipboard-to-Run execution: RunMRU write + shell spawned from explorer AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the host-side artifact of DOUBLECUP's fake-CAPTCHA social engineering — the victim pasting the clipboard-staged command into the Win+R Run dialog. Detects the HKCU RunMRU value (and/or explorer spawning a shell) carrying the cache-search command. Article-specific: the copied command references certutil/findstr and the PNG cache. Rationale: The RunMRU key is the canonical forensic residue of the ClickFix 'paste into Run dialog' lure the article describes ('command automatically copied to their clipboard'). Constraining the value to certutil/findstr/.png/Cache ties it to this specific campaign rather than generic RunMRU noise. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually running a diagnostic command via Win+R that references a cache path
  • Power user pasting a legitimate PowerShell one-liner into Run
  • IT script that pre-seeds RunMRU for a curl/PowerShell task
  • Browser troubleshooting steps that clear .png cache via Run
  • Software installer that shells out through explorer
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full RunMRU value and correlate to the immediately-following process tree (explorer -> cmd/powershell -> certutil/findstr). Interview the user — ClickFix victims recall a 'CAPTCHA fix' instruction. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the chain, and reset the user's session/credentials if a stealer stage ran. 3) Hunt: pivot to browser-cache PNG extraction (UC2), public-IP-keyed decryption (UC4), and the spoofed-SaaS domain the user visited (UC1).
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Explorer\RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("powershell","cmd","certutil","findstr","curl","mshta",".png","Cache")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Explorer\RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("powershell","cmd","certutil","findstr","curl","mshta",".png","Cache")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Public-IPv4 discovery by non-browser process (environmental keying for payload decryption) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts DOUBLECUP's second-stage dropper retrieving the victim's public IPv4 to derive the SHA-256/CTR-XOR decryption key for the final payload. Detects a non-browser process resolving a public-IP-echo service — the environmental-keying tell that precedes in-memory execution. Article-specific per SOCRadar's IP-as-key analysis. Rationale: Encodes the article/SOCRadar detail that the dropper 'retrieves the victim's public IPv4 address and uses it to create a decryption key' via a SHA-256 CTR/XOR scheme. A non-browser process hitting an IP-echo service is the observable proxy for that keying step. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/doublecup-uses-clickfix-and-cached-pngs.html

DeviceManager EtherHiding: non-browser host querying Ethereum/Polygon RPC endpoints for C2 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts DeviceManager RAT resolving its live C2 IP from an Ethereum/Polygon smart contract (EtherHiding). Detects a non-developer/non-browser host reaching public blockchain RPC providers — a decentralized dead-drop resolver that resists takedown. Article-specific: SOCRadar attributes this exact EtherHiding C2-resolution behaviour to DeviceManager. Rationale: The article states DeviceManager 'uses a technique known as EtherHiding to retrieve its current C2 address from an Ethereum or Polygon smart contract.' A non-browser/non-dev process resolving public blockchain RPC providers is the network observable of that dead-drop resolver. Corroborated by SOCRadar and The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/doublecup-uses-clickfix-and-cached-pngs.html

DeviceManager DNS A/TXT tunneling for command retrieval and data exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts DeviceManager's DNS-based C2/exfil channel — using A and TXT records to pull commands, stage payloads, and beacon out stolen system data. Detects abnormal TXT-query volume per host and Python-driven DNS beaconing (DeviceManager is a Python RAT). Article-specific per SOCRadar's DNS A/TXT C2 analysis. Rationale: Encodes the article's statement that DeviceManager 'uses DNS A and TXT records to steal system information, retrieve commands to execute, download payloads, and send command output.' High per-host TXT volume + Python-driven DNS beaconing are the two orthogonal observables of that channel. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/doublecup-uses-clickfix-and-cached-pngs.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Email-security gateways doing bulk SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT lookups
  • Certificate automation (ACME/DNS-01) issuing TXT queries
  • Python monitoring scripts performing frequent DNS lookups
  • Security scanners enumerating TXT records
  • Service-discovery tools polling DNS-SD TXT records
Suppression filter
| where not (SampleName has_any ("_dmarc","_domainkey","_acme-challenge","spf"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the queried domains and TXT payloads for base64/hex-encoded blobs and abnormally long labels; benign TXT (SPF/DMARC/ACME) is short and to well-known apex domains. Confirm the initiating process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the tunneling domain/resolver, and preserve the Python process/memory. 3) Hunt: pivot to the EtherHiding C2 resolution (UC5), the IPv4-keyed decrypt (UC4), and the original ClickFix delivery domain (UC1) to scope the full chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| summarize DnsConnCount = count(), DistinctResolvers = dcount(RemoteIP), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where DnsConnCount > 100  // 100 = well above benign python DNS/day; DeviceManager beacons far more
| order by DnsConnCount desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where QueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize TxtQueryCount = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(Name), SampleName = any(Name), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, ClientIP
| where TxtQueryCount > 50  // 50 = P99 TXT lookups/host/day; benign hosts issue <10
| order by TxtQueryCount desc

CountLoader macOS LaunchAgent recon: sw_vers/system_profiler/ioreg clustered under one parent AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the macOS CountLoader variant that fingerprints the host with built-in utilities (sw_vers, system_profiler, ioreg, curl) before installing a LaunchAgent for persistence. Detects three-or-more of these recon binaries spawned by one non-interactive parent. Article-specific: SOCRadar names this exact utility set for the Intel/Apple-Silicon CountLoader build. Rationale: Directly uses the article's named macOS recon set ('built-in utilities such as curl, sw_vers, system_profiler, and ioreg') plus LaunchAgent persistence. Clustering ≥3 of these under one non-shell parent distinguishes malware fingerprinting from an admin typing them interactively. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/doublecup-clickfix-loader-devicemanager-rats/
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1082 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MDM/RMM inventory agents (Jamf, Kandji) enumerating hardware
  • Legitimate installers running system_profiler for compatibility checks
  • IT diagnostic scripts run over SSH
  • Asset-management tooling collecting ioreg/sw_vers output
  • Developer build scripts probing the host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/Library/Application Support/JAMF" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jamf","kandji-daemon","osqueryd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and whether it is signed/notarized; a curl call to an unknown host immediately after the recon cluster is the malicious tell. Check ~/Library/LaunchAgents for a new plist. 2) Contain: isolate the Mac, remove the malicious LaunchAgent plist, and kill the parent process. 3) Hunt: review outbound curl destinations for C2, and check for the CountLoader Windows path (scheduled tasks, browser-wallet/extension enumeration) across the fleet. Sentinel/Datadog left empty — this tenant has no macOS EDR table equivalent to MDE DeviceProcessEvents.

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc

description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
